heading: Section 1 — Welcome
text: Section 1 — Welcome Welcome to the team. This document explains how the job works — what you'll be doing, how to do it well, and who to ask when something doesn't match what you expected. Read it before your first shift. Keep it after.

heading: 1.1 — Who you work for
text: You work for The Retail Odyssey Company . That's the name on your badge. Two things still carry an older name, and they're the two you'll hit first: Where you'll see it What it says The Field App prod.sasretail.com HR paperwork and payroll May reference SAS Retail Services Here's the structure: Retail Odyssey is a division of SAS Retail Services, and both are owned by Advantage Solutions. SAS spun Retail Odyssey off a few years ago. Badges have moved over; some systems still carry the older name because renaming a login domain is harder than renaming a company. None of this affects your job. It's here so you don't spend your first week wondering whether you were hired by two different employers.

heading: 1.2 — Where you work
text: You'll be working in Fred Meyer stores. Fred Meyer is a division of Kroger. Retail Odyssey serves other retailers, and their programs run differently. Everything in this document describes Fred Meyer work specifically. If you're ever scheduled outside Fred Meyer, ask me first — don't assume any of this carries over.

heading: 1.3 — What the job actually is
text: You are a Retail Reset Merchandiser . Typically once a week, a team goes into a store and rebuilds shelf sections to a new plan — new products in, discontinued products out, shelves moved, labels replaced. Sometimes, as the situation calls for it, we'll be in the same store multiple days in a week. The program that governs this work at Fred Meyer is called Kompass , and Section 2 explains it properly. It's the first thing to read after this page, because every other section assumes you know what it is. A few things worth knowing up front: The work is physical. You're standing, lifting, and reaching for most of a shift. The work is precise. A shelf is either set to the planogram or it isn't. There's no partial credit on a facing count. The work is visible. The section you build is what customers shop for the next several months. That's the appeal of it, and it's also why the details matter.

heading: 1.4 — Who to ask
text: Situation Who Anything during a shift Your Team Lead — they're on site with you Scheduling, pay, assignments, anything your lead can't resolve Me — I'm your supervisor Accommodations, benefits, employment paperwork HR , or start with me and I'll route you Your lead is your first call for essentially everything on the floor. Asking is not an imposition — a question costs a minute, and a section set wrong costs an afternoon. You will not be expected to know things nobody told you. If this document doesn't cover it, that's a gap in the document, and I'd like to hear about it.

heading: 1.5 — How to use this document
text: Before your first shift, read Sections 1 through 6. They cover what to wear, what to bring, how to log in, how to arrive, and how to work safely. Before your first reset, read the rest of Part I. It covers how to read a planogram, how to perform a reset, and how to close one out. Part II is reference, not reading. Don't work through it. It's there for when you meet something you don't recognize — a fixture, a term, a department that works differently. Glossary, special fixtures, storage, conditioning by department, front end, aisle navigation , bakery, shelf hardware, and the commodity list. The last section is a quick-reference card. Print it and keep it with your tools — the reset steps, the pull categories, and who to ask for what, on one page. Two sections are worth rereading after you've worked a shift or two, because they'll make more sense once you've seen the shelf: Section 2 (Kompass) and Section 7 (Reading a Planogram) .

heading: 2.1 — The name
text: KOMPASS stands for K roger O ptimization M anagement P lan A ligning S tore S ales. It's Kroger's program for keeping shelf sets current — making sure what's on the shelf matches what Kroger has planned for it. New products go in, discontinued products come out, and the layout gets rebuilt to a new plan. You will hear this word constantly. Every reset you work, every note you're handed, every cart you pull from — Kompass. It is the name of the job you were hired to do. Scope: everything in this document describes Kompass work at Fred Meyer , a division of Kroger. Retail Odyssey serves other retailers, and their programs run differently. If you're ever assigned outside Fred Meyer, ask me before assuming any of this carries over.

heading: 2.2 — How the week works
text: Kompass typically runs on a weekly visit to each store. Some weeks the work calls for more — expect to be in the same store multiple days when the volume requires it. The work is split between two sides: Side Who What they own Store The Kompass Champion — usually the Operations Assistant Store Manager Preps the store ahead of the visit, supports the team during it, signs off on completed work Vendor — us The Retail Odyssey Kompass Team Executes resets, new item introductions, and maintenances against current planograms; walks the finished work with the store and provides sign-off sheets What that looks like in practice: a dedicated Kompass Champion is rarely staffed in stores anymore. Most of the prep, organization, and sign-off coordination has shifted onto our team and your lead. You should expect to absorb work the store standard says belongs to the store. That is not a complaint and it is not a reason to skip steps. The formal split still exists, and your lead uses it to set expectations during the walk-through. But if you arrive expecting someone to have staged everything for you, you'll be surprised. Plan to find things yourself and ask your lead when you can't.

heading: 2.3 — What the store is supposed to have ready
text: Knowing this list tells you what to look for when you arrive, and what to flag when it's missing: Kompass Notes for the week, printed and filed Kompass tags , filed by the store's Price Changer ahead of the visit The Vestcom box , located and secured — this arrives by FedEx each week and holds your planograms, strips, and tags The Kompass cart , organized and accessible, holding only the new items for this visit Cleaning supplies , stocked and ready A designated spot for perishable and frozen new items Data Skins , enough on hand for upcoming resets Missing or wrong? Tell your lead. Planogram problems get escalated ahead of the visit where possible.

heading: 2.4 — The two kinds of work
text: Not every Kompass project is a full teardown. Know which one you've been assigned before you start pulling product.

heading: Full Reset — "Kompass Updates"
text: The whole category is rebuilt to a new planogram. Pull all discontinued items per the Kompass Notes — they carry closeout tags — and route them to the store associate or into clearly labeled boxes Pull the existing strips from the set and install the new ones Set the entire category to the new planogram Rotate stock properly: older product to the front, newer product to the back of each facing Pull all new-item stock from the back room onto the shelf Wipe down all moved shelving and tag moldings Hang every tag provided; hand-write tags where the store needs to recreate them Move backstock to the designated associate or into labeled overstock boxes

heading: Partial — NIIs & Maintenances
text: Only part of the set changes. The discipline here is restraint — you touch what changed and nothing else. Pull discontinued items per the Kompass Notes, same as a full reset Replace strips only on the shelves that changed — not the whole set Set only the changing area of the planogram to the new strips Where a category has no strips, cut the new items into the set per the planogram Wipe down only the affected shelves — not the entire set Hang every tag provided, or hand-write for the store to recreate Move backstock to the designated associate or labeled overstock boxes Both types share one constant: keep the aisle shoppable the entire time. Materials, baskets, and carts stay on one side so customers always have a clear path through.

heading: 2.5 — The shelf edge: data skins, strips, and tags
text: Three separate things live on the front edge of the shelf, and new hires mix them up constantly. Learn the difference before your first reset. Part What it is Data skin The clear plastic channel guide that snaps onto the front edge of the shelf. It's the hardware — it holds everything else Strip The printed label strip that slides into the data skin Tag The individual price tag for a single product The order is physical: skin snaps to the shelf, strip slides into the skin, tags sit on the strip. Why this matters on the job: a strip has nowhere to go if the data skin is missing, damaged, or the wrong size. On a full reset you're replacing every strip on the set, so damaged skins turn up as you work. On an NII or maintenance you're only touching the shelves that changed — but a bad skin on one of those shelves still stops you. Correcting data skins is part of NII and DI work. If you're short, tell your lead — the store is supposed to keep enough on hand for upcoming resets, and reorders get coordinated through the Kompass Team.

heading: 2.6 — Rotation
text: On every set you touch, older stock goes to the front and newer stock goes to the back of each facing. This is proper Key Retailing rotation, and it is not optional. The reason is simple: product that sits behind newer stock ages out and becomes a loss for the store. A perfectly set shelf with reversed rotation is a shelf that will generate out-of-code product in a few weeks.

heading: 2.7 — Closing out the visit
text: Your lead drives this, but you should know the sequence: Notify the Kompass Champion or Food Manager with an estimated completion time Complete the sign-off sheets — one for the store, plus a Summary Sign-Off for the Champion or Food Manager to sign Capture the signature — signing means the store agrees the work is complete to standard. Photograph the signed Summary page Walk every project with the store — show them where all overstock and discontinued items ended up Hand off — leave a copy of the completed sign-off sheets for the store's records Sign-off methods are in flux right now. Both fax and photo are in use — your lead will tell you which applies to your assignment.

heading: 2.8 — Fred Meyer systems: what you sign, and what you don't
text: CAO and Kompass Completion are Fred Meyer systems. They're the technology the store uses to sign out completed work at the end of a visit. Retail Odyssey employees do not have logins to either one, and are not permitted to sign work out in them. That's not a local rule or a matter of seniority — no one on our side has that access, including your lead and including me. Here's the clean division: Record Who owns it Sign-off sheets and the Summary Sign-Off page Us — your lead prepares them, the store signs them, we keep a photo Entry in CAO / Kompass Completion The store, always So the sequence at the end of a visit is: we produce the paperwork, the store manager signs it, and the store enters it in their system on their own. If a store associate asks you to enter something for them, the answer is that you don't have access — point them to your lead. Our paperwork is our proof the work was done. Theirs is theirs.

heading: 2.9 — Who to contact
text: Situation Route Planogram discrepancy found ahead of the visit Kompass Managers or Kompass Merchandising Support Anything on the day of the visit Your Team Lead — the Lead routes to me You're not sure which applies Your Team Lead Your lead is your first call for essentially everything. That's what they're there for.

heading: 2.10 — Vocabulary
text: You'll hear all of these in your first week: Term Meaning Kompass Champion The store's designated contact for the visit, usually the Operations Assistant Store Manager Kompass Notes The weekly instructions for what's changing at this store Kompass cart The store's staging cart holding new items for the visit Vestcom box The weekly FedEx shipment containing planograms, strips, and tags Data Skin The clear channel guide that snaps onto the front edge of the shelf. The strip slides into it Strip The printed shelf-edge label strip that slides into the data skin and carries the tags Gondola The shelving unit that holds the shelves — the structure you set NII New Item Introduction — adding new products to an existing set DI Discontinued Item — flagged in the Notes and carrying a closeout tag Maintenance A partial project correcting or updating part of a set Backstock / overstock Product left over after the set is complete Kompass Completion The store's system for confirming work — store access only Key Retailing Kroger's operating standards, including stock rotation

heading: Section 3 — Before Your First Shift
text: Section 3 — Before Your First Shift Two things to handle before you show up: get your tools, and get into the Field App . Neither takes long, and both are difficult to sort out on the morning of your first assignment.

heading: 3.1 — Your tool kit
text: You supply these yourself. They're yours, you bring them to every assignment, and you're responsible for keeping them in working condition. Tool What it's for Tape measure, 12 ft or longer Shelf heights and section footage. A short tape covers the heights but won't measure a 20-foot section, and confirming footage is the first check you make on any set . Get one that's easy to read Screwdrivers — Phillips and flat head Shelf hardware, brackets, and pegboard mounting Pliers Stubborn clips, bent hardware, and anything a screwdriver won't turn Box cutter Opening boxes of new items Spare blades Dull blades are a hazard, not an inconvenience. Replace them often Safety gloves Required for frozen resets, and any time the store requires them Scraper Removing old tags and stubborn dirt from shelves and moldings Permanent marker Labeling boxes and hand-writing shelf tags Pen Notes, and anything the marker is too heavy for Highlighter Marking positions on the planogram. When you can't tag a position, you highlight it and hand the planogram to your lead — Section 8 , Step 8 Scissors Trimming strips, opening packaging a blade would tear Scotch tape Temporary fixes on strips and tags until the real replacement arrives Strongly recommended, not required: Knee pads or a kneeling mat You set bottom shelf first and work up, so you start every bay on the floor. Six bays into a shift, this is the difference between a good day and a bad back. Get them before your first assignment rather than after the shift that convinces you A box cutter, not a pocketknife. No folding knives, no switch-style knives, nothing that isn't a purpose-built retractable box cutter. A blade you can't retract in the half-second before you set it down is a blade that finds someone, and a pocketknife in a store also reads very differently to a customer than a box cutter does. None of this is expensive. The whole kit is available cheaply, and it's yours for as long as you look after it.

heading: 3.2 — Setting up the Field App
text: The Field App is where your schedule lives. Get into it before your first shift, not during it. The address is prod.sasretail.com/en/field. Yes, it says SAS. Section 1.1 covers why. It's the right address. You'll also hear it called Retail Logic or the SAS Retail App — that's the same tool under its official names. Most people just say the Field App. It runs in a browser on any web-enabled device — computer, tablet, or phone. Bookmark it. You'll open it constantly and typing that URL gets old fast. What it does for you: Shows your schedule and any new assignments Tells you which store you're assigned to Gives you your lead's name Estimates your drive time to the store Carries any special instructions for your assignment Log in every day. Assignments get added, and special instructions post there. Checking daily is the difference between knowing where you're going tomorrow and finding out tomorrow.

heading: Your company ID
text: Your login is your official company ID . It's typically formatted firstname.lastname@youradv.com — the "youradv" part is Your Advantage. Not every ID follows that pattern, so variations do occur. Yours is in your welcome email — use exactly what it gives you.

heading: How much of it to type
text: You'll hit more than one login screen, and they don't all want the same thing. Look at the screen you're on: If the login screen says Type Microsoft The whole thing — firstname.lastname@youradv.com Advantage, SAS, or Retail Odyssey Just firstname.lastname — no @youradv.com That one detail accounts for most failed logins. If you're getting rejected with credentials you know are right, check which screen you're looking at before you do anything else.

heading: Your password
text: It's the same password you set up with Oracle during onboarding. Not a separate one, not one that came in an email — the Oracle password.

heading: Getting your credentials
text: Your login information comes to your personal email — the address you gave HR. Watch for a welcome message once your onboarding steps are complete. It contains the link and your username. Didn't get it? Check spam first — it's usually there. Still nothing, contact me and I'll get it to you.

heading: 3.4 — A note on phones
text: You need a device to reach the Field App, and for most people that's a phone. That's fine — but understand how the two rules fit together. Check the app before your shift, not during it. On the sales floor, personal phones stay silenced and out of sight. Leads carry a phone for the app and for coordination; merchandisers don't. Section 4 covers this properly. So: look at your schedule and instructions in the morning, or the night before. Confirm your hours at the end of the day, after your shift. Not in the aisle.

heading: 3.5 — Before your first assignment
text: Work through this list: Tool kit purchased — 12 ft tape measure, screwdrivers, pliers, box cutter, spare blades, gloves, scraper, marker, pen, highlighter, scissors, scotch tape Knee pads or a kneeling mat — not required, but get them Field App bookmarked on the device you'll use Logged in successfully at least once Schedule checked — you know the store, the date, and your start time Lead's name noted Drive time checked, with margin for traffic and weather Polo and badge ready, pants and shoes meeting the dress code in Section 4 Read Sections 4 through 6 If any of these won't come together in time, tell me before your shift rather than after.

heading: Section 4 — Professional Standards
text: Section 4 — Professional Standards You represent Retail Odyssey inside someone else's store. To the customers around you, you're indistinguishable from staff — which means how you present affects both companies at once. Most of what follows is straightforward. The parts that surprise people are the phone rule, the bag rule, and the receipt rule, so read those closely.

heading: 4.1 — What to wear
text: Required on every assignment: Item Standard Polo Company-issued. Wear it Name badge Your Retail Odyssey badge, clipped to your shirt, name clearly visible Pants Solid blue, solid black, or plain khaki. No more than one inch above the ankle Shoes Completely closed, clean, and skid-resistant Optional: A solid-colored long-sleeve shirt under your polo For refrigerated or frozen work: a solid-colored, logo-free sweater, sweatshirt, or jacket in blue, black, or gray On shoes — closed and skid-resistant isn't only about looking professional. You'll be on hard floors, around dropped product and spills, moving carts and hand trucks. This is a safety requirement wearing a dress-code hat.

heading: 4.2 — What not to wear
text: Pants and clothing: Shorts, capri pants, sweatpants, yoga pants Anything faded, torn, baggy, or tight Colored patterns, logos, or writing Footwear: Boots, with the exception of work boots Everything else: Sunglasses Headphones and music devices — see 4.4 If you're unsure whether something you own meets the standard, ask me before your shift rather than finding out at the store. Appearance standards beyond the dress code above — anything this section doesn't cover — are in your employee handbook.

heading: 4.3 — Grooming
text: Neat, clean, and ready to work. That's the whole standard. You'll be within a few feet of customers for most of a shift, often reaching across them or working beside them in a narrow aisle.

heading: 4.4 — Headphones and music devices
text: Headphones are not allowed on the sales floor. Not any kind, not at any point during your assignment. This is the rule people test most, so here is exactly what it covers: Both earbuds, or one earbud Wired or wireless Over-ear, on-ear, in-ear, bone conduction Under a hood, under a hat, or under your hair Playing nothing at all If it sits on or in your ear, it comes out before you walk onto the floor. Music devices are covered too , headphones or not. No speakers, no radios, no phone playing out loud — anywhere in the store, including the back room . The store controls the sound in its own building. Why this one isn't negotiable. You work in an aisle where carts, hand trucks, and pallet jacks move behind you. A customer trying to get past you, a teammate calling a warning, a store announcement, the sound of something falling — you need all of it. Every reset injury that starts with "I didn't hear it coming" starts here. The second reason is simpler: someone wearing headphones reads as unavailable. Customers won't approach you and store staff won't either, and part of your job is being approachable to both. Expect this to be enforced. Your lead will ask you to remove them. Repeated after that, it becomes a conversation with me. I'd rather it never gets that far, so treat this as settled before your first shift.

heading: 4.5 — Phones
text: Merchandisers: your personal phone stays on vibrate and out of sight for your entire assignment — including when you're walking through the store on a break. Leads: carry a phone for the Field App and for coordinating the team. That's a working tool, not an exception to the rule. When a phone does come out, three conditions hold for everyone: On vibrate. Never on a ring tone, never on speaker Business use only while you're in the store Never while you're moving product. Stop, put down what you're carrying, then look at the phone. A hand on a phone is a hand not on the cart, the ladder, or the shelf you're loading A call you genuinely have to take is a call you take outside, on a break. Why it's written this way. A customer or store employee who sees you on a device reads it as you not working. They don't know whether you're checking a planogram or checking a text, and they don't stop to find out — they form an impression of Retail Odyssey and pass it to the store. That impression is the entire reason the rule exists. Practical version: check the Field App before your shift and after it. Not in the aisle. Section 3.4 covers the timing.

heading: 4.6 — Personal items
text: Purses, handbags, backpacks, and tote bags don't come into the store. Leave them locked in your vehicle. This isn't about trust. You're a non-employee moving through a building full of merchandise all day, and a bag you're carrying is a question nobody should have to ask you. Not carrying one means it never comes up. What you do bring — coat, lunch, tools — goes in the area your lead designates at the start of the shift. Ask where it is before you need it, not while you're holding it.

heading: 4.7 — Eating, drinking, and purchases
text: No food or drink on the sales floor. None, at any point. Not a coffee on a shelf, not a water bottle in a cart, not something in your hand while you walk. A drink set down on a shelf gets knocked into product, and a customer who sees you eating in an aisle sees a store that lets people eat in aisles. Eat before you arrive. Eating and drinking are permitted during lunch or a scheduled break, in the designated areas only. Ask your lead where those are on your first shift. If you buy something in the store during your shift: Pay for it before you consume any part of it — food, drink, or product Keep the receipt until the end of your shift Be ready to show it to store staff on the way out, or any time you're asked That last one catches people. It isn't an accusation and it isn't personal — you're a non-employee carrying store merchandise, and the receipt is what makes that unremarkable. Keep it in a pocket, not in a cart you're going to return.

heading: 4.8 — Customers
text: Customers will mistake you for store staff. It happens constantly and it's a compliment to how you look. If someone asks you for help, help them if you can. Point them to the right aisle, hand them something off a high shelf, find them a store employee. If it's beyond what you can do, walk them to someone who can rather than sending them off with a direction. Be respectful of the store and everyone in it at all times. You're a guest with a badge.

heading: 4.9 — Variations and accommodations
text: Some dress guidelines vary by program. If you work an assignment with a different standard, you'll be told. If you're unsure which applies, ask me. If you need an accommodation for any reason, talk to me or to HR directly. Either route is fine, and you don't need to explain yourself to anyone else on the team.

heading: Section 5 — Arriving at the Store
text: Section 5 — Arriving at the Store The first twenty minutes of a shift set up everything after it. Arrive on time, check in with the right person, and get your materials to the aisle in one organized trip or two — and the reset starts clean.

heading: 5.1 — Getting there
text: Check the Field App the night before. It gives you the store, your start time, your lead's name, and an estimated drive time. Treat that estimate as a floor, not a plan. It doesn't know about traffic, weather, or the fact that you'll need time to park and walk in. Add margin. Arriving on time matters more here than in most jobs. A reset team works as a unit — your lead assigns projects at check-in, and one person arriving late holds up the assignment for everyone else, not just themselves. If you're going to be late, tell your lead as early as you know. Not when you arrive.

heading: 5.2 — Parking
text: Park near the back of the lot. The spaces closest to the store belong to customers. This is one of the easiest things to get right and one of the most visible things to get wrong — store management notices vendor vehicles in the good spots, and they remember. Factor the walk from the back of the lot into your arrival time. Your lead or I will tell you how to get in. Don't guess and don't default to the front doors. It's usually the grocery receiving door — the loading dock at the back where the semis back up to unload. Beside the dock there's a normal person-sized door, called the man door . That's the one drivers use, and it's the one we use. No one comes with you. Not children, not family, not a friend waiting inside. The store is a workplace and you're there as a vendor — anyone who isn't working the project doesn't come in.

heading: 5.3 — Checking in
text: You check in with your lead. They'll be at the front of the store. Your lead checks in with the store — with the Kompass Champion or, more often, the Food Manager. That's their job, not yours. You don't need to find store management on arrival. Your lead will: Give you any last-minute instructions Assign you to your project for the day Walk you through the store if you're new to it Introduce you to the store staff you'll need Have you grab a shopping cart for your equipment and materials If something looks wrong — a planogram that doesn't match, missing materials, a section that isn't what the assignment says — tell your lead. They route it from there. Discrepancies go up through the lead to me, not directly from you to store management.

heading: 5.4 — Who's who in the store
text: You'll deal with three store roles regularly. Knowing which one to ask saves a lot of walking. Who What they handle You'll need them for Store Manager Overall store operations; final walk-through and sign-off Your lead handles this. Let them know what you're working on if you're introduced Price changer (also called the scan or pricing coordinator) Shelf tags, pricing, shelf strips Missing tags, tags that don't match, replacement strips. A position you couldn't tag goes to your lead, who brings it here Receiver ( back room ) Incoming product and equipment New-item stock, hand trucks, dollies, U-boats, boxes and milk crates Your lead is still your first call. This table is so you understand who does what, not an instruction to go around your lead. When your lead sends you to the scan coordinator for a missing tag, this is why.

heading: 5.5 — Getting your materials to the aisle
text: Your working materials come from the Kompass cart — Kompass Notes , planograms, strips, and tags for the week's projects. Your lead will point you to it. For everything else, the receiver is the source: new-item stock, boxes and crates, and a hand truck, dolly, or U-boat if you need one to move product. Loading: Put your equipment in the cart first, then your materials on top of it Don't overload. Make as many trips as it takes Use a hand truck or dolly for anything heavy rather than stacking the cart high Multiple trips are not inefficiency. An overloaded cart is how product gets damaged, how equipment gets dropped, and how someone gets hurt navigating a corner. The trip back to the aisle costs a minute; a broken case costs more than that. If something you need isn't there — no strips, no cleaning supplies, no boxes — tell your lead. Don't improvise around it and don't buy it yourself.

heading: 5.6 — Before you start setting
text: Once you're at your section with your materials, Section 8.2 picks up: check the planogram version and effective date , read the Kompass Notes, measure the section, count the shelves, and stage your boxes. Do that before anything comes off a shelf.

heading: Section 6 — Working Safely
text: Section 6 — Working Safely This is the longest section in the document, and it's the one worth reading twice. Reset work puts you on hard floors, up on step stools, around moving equipment, and with a blade in your hand — usually all in the same shift. Nothing here is complicated. Almost all of it is the kind of thing you already know and skip when you're moving fast.

heading: 6.1 — If you see something unsafe, say so immediately
text: Contact your lead the moment you notice a hazard — to you, to a teammate, to a store employee, or to a customer. Not at the end of the shift. Not after you've worked around it. Immediately. This includes things that aren't your problem and things you didn't cause: a damaged ceiling panel, a leaking case, a broken step stool, a fixture that moves when it shouldn't. You are not being difficult by reporting it. You're the person who happened to be standing there.

heading: 6.2 — Working smart
text: Most of this is attention rather than procedure. Don't stand in front of swinging doors. Someone is coming through, and they can't see you Slow down at blind corners — especially pushing a cart or carrying boxes Use handrails on stairs. Turn the lights on in stairwells and any enclosed area before entering Read warning and directional signs. They're posted because something happened Never stack anything next to or in front of an electrical service panel. It has to stay clear Use tools only as they're intended. A scraper is not a pry bar and a cutter is not a screwdriver

heading: 6.3 — Working clean
text: Keep your aisle clear. Carts, boxes, crates, and materials stay on one side so customers always have a path through. This is a safety rule before it's a service rule — a blocked aisle is where people trip and where carts collide. If something breaks, deal with it right then: Clean up the spill or damage immediately Mark the area until the floor is properly cleaned and no longer slippery Report it to your lead. Working alone, report it to the store manager or receiver Finding something to mark it with. We don't carry cones. Stores usually keep collapsible canvas cones tucked away at the ends of the aisles — behind an end cap, sometimes sitting on top of one. Look there first. If you can't find one, post something at the spot — or someone. Depending on the situation that might be a cart, a box, or a person standing there until it's handled. What it is matters less than that the hazard is visibly marked and nobody walks into it. Don't leave a wet floor unmarked, don't leave it unattended, and don't assume a store employee saw it. Handling trash: Assume there's broken glass or something sharp in the bag, because eventually there will be Hold trash away from your body Never push down on a bag to compress it Use a container to move trash whenever you can

heading: 6.4 — Lifting, and moving shelving
text: Before you lift anything: Plan the move first. Look at the pathway and the destination. Contorting yourself around clutter halfway through a lift is how backs go Test the load by lifting one side first Uneven or unstable? Redistribute it, or get help Too heavy? Split it into smaller loads, get a second person, or use a handling aid The lift itself: Wide stance — feet at least shoulder width, one foot forward and to the side of the load Back straight, knees bent, buttocks pushed out. Picture a weightlifter Load as close to your body as you can get it. Distance from your body is what multiplies weight onto your spine Head forward , so your spine stays aligned Breathe out as you lift Never twist. Turn with your feet — pivot, don't rotate your torso under load Twisting under load is the single most common way people hurt themselves doing this job, and it happens because turning your feet feels slower. It isn't. It's a half second. Two people lifting: talk to each other. Agree who lifts on what count, which way you're going, and where you're setting it down. Poor coordination is what turns a two-person lift into a one-person lift halfway across the floor. Above shoulder height: use a step stool or ladder. Never a box, a crate, or a shelf. See 6.6 . Moving product off a shelf or rack: move it laterally to a nearby surface rather than lifting it down and away. Less distance under load, less reaching. Never lift more than you're sure you can. Ask for help — nobody thinks less of you for it, and everybody thinks less of a back injury that was avoidable On shelving specifically: Never lean a shelf up against something and leave it unattended. Accidents happen fast, and there is no stable or safe position for a shelf other than locked into the gondola . Gondola is the term for the shelving unit that holds the shelves — the whole structure you're working on. You'll hear it constantly, so learn it now. If a shelf is out, it is either in your hands or locked back into the gondola. There is no third state.

heading: 6.5 — Safety cutters
text: You'll use one regularly, and familiarity is exactly what makes it dangerous. Keep your free hand as far from the blade as possible Hold the box firmly so it can't shift while you cut Look at what you're cutting. Most cutter injuries happen to someone who was looking somewhere else Replace dull blades often. A dull blade requires force, force slips, and slips cut people. A dull blade is more dangerous than a sharp one Dispose of used blades properly — never in a trash bag someone else will lift Carry and store it closed

heading: 6.6 — Reaching high shelves
text: A step stool or step ladder is the only approved way to reach a top shelf. Not a milk crate, not a shelf, not a cart, not anything else that happens to be nearby.

heading: Before you step on it
text: Check the stool or ladder every time: Rungs and steps undamaged Braces and feet intact No loose parts Nothing slippery on the steps or surfaces Damaged? Don't use it. Remove it from the work area so nobody else picks it up, and report it to your lead or the store manager immediately.

heading: Setting it up
text: Dry, level surface. Never on top of something else Completely open, with the spreaders locked Check the weight capacity — it has to hold you and whatever you're carrying Never in front of a door that isn't locked, blocked, or guarded Never against a window

heading: On it
text: Keep your body centered. If you're leaning to reach, get down and move it Always come down before repositioning it Never move a ladder with a person or equipment on it Never reach for a shelf higher than you can see. If you can't see the shelf, you can't see what's on it or what you're about to knock off it

heading: 6.7 — Cold work
text: Wear your safety gloves for every frozen reset, and any time the store requires them. Cold makes your hands clumsy and slow before it makes them cold enough to notice. Gloves are as much about grip and dexterity as they are about temperature. If it came out of a refrigerator or freezer, it goes back into one. That's a product rule, but it's in this section because the temptation to leave a case out "just for a minute" is what turns into a full pallet of loss.

heading: 6.8 — If you get hurt
text: Emergency: call 911. Don't hesitate, and don't wait to ask anyone first. For anything else, there's a process, and the first step of it is on a clock. 1 Within 24 hours of the injury , report the claim to the Workers' Compensation Intake Call Center — 888-900-4276, option 3, then option 1 2 See the in-network doctor you're referred to 3 Send your doctor's restrictions to the workers' comp department after the appointment — email or fax 4 Contact WC Claims to build a return-to-work or accommodation plan 5 Always tell your supervisor. Whatever else happens, and whoever else you've spoken to Go to every follow-up appointment. Missed appointments are the most common way a straightforward claim turns into a difficult one. The 24 hours is the part that matters most. A report inside 24 hours is routine. A report after it is a claim someone has to justify, and you're the one being asked to justify it — weeks later, about an injury you're still recovering from. New injury or illness 888-900-4276 — option 3, then option 1 Follow up on an existing claim 888-900-4276 — option 3, then option 2 Safety concern, or escalate a serious event 888-900-4276 — option 3, then option 3 Submit documents workerscompensation.claims@yourADV.com · fax 858-431-1158 Safety department 888-900-4276, options 3 then 3 · safety@yourADV.com Human resources 855-472-8276, option 4 Report it even if you think it's nothing. The injuries that turn into problems are almost never the dramatic ones — they're the ones somebody worked through for a week first.

heading: 6.9 — Equipment
text: Equipment you may use: Hand trucks, dollies, U-boats, and manual pallet jacks — following all posted safety guidelines. They are always walked , whether loaded or empty Never ride one, and never let anyone else ride one Equipment you do not operate, ever: Electric pallet jacks Forklifts Only store employees are authorized to operate powered equipment. If someone asks you to move something with a powered jack, the answer is that you're not authorized. Find your lead. Balers: two conditions, both required. You must be 18 or older to operate a baler You must be shown how to use that specific baler before you use it Posted directions on the machine are not training. If nobody has walked you through that baler, don't operate it — ask your lead. Once you have been shown, follow the posted safety guidelines exactly.

heading: Section 7 — How to Read a Planogram
text: Section 7 — How to Read a Planogram A planogram — often called a POG or a schematic — is the map for your assignment. It tells you what goes on the shelf, exactly where, and how many. You do not guess, and you do not improve on it. If the shelf can't match the planogram, you stop and contact me. Everything below uses a real Fred Meyer set you may actually be assigned to.

heading: 7.1 — Reading the file name
text: Your assignment arrives with a name that looks like nonsense. It isn't. Here's the one we're using: D701_L00000_D03_C166_V689_F020_MX — HP 72IN HAIR CARE PREMIUM (FM) Piece Meaning D701 Division 701 — Fred Meyer L00000 Location code; all zeros means the set is standard across stores, not store-specific D03 Department 03 — HBC (Health & Beauty Care) C166 Commodity 166 — Hair Care Products V689 Version 689 of this planogram F020 The size of the set — 20 feet. This field isn't always feet; see below MX Store format — the multi-department format covering both the grocery and home sides of the store HP 72IN 72-inch fixture height (FM) Fred Meyer Three of these matter more than the rest. Check all three before you touch anything. Check Why Category — C166 Tells you which set you're holding. The single most common way to start the wrong job is to pick up the right-looking planogram for the wrong commodity Size — F020 Twenty feet. This has to match the section in front of you. It's the first physical check you make, and it's in 8.2 for exactly that reason Version — V689 How you know the plan is current. Planograms get revised. If your version doesn't match what your lead is working from, stop and ask before you set anything Category tells you what , size tells you whether it fits , and version tells you whether it's still true. Any one of the three being wrong means you're about to do work that has to be undone. Size isn't always in feet. Read the letter before the number. Prefix Unit Example Where you'll see it F Feet F020 — 20 feet Most sets D Doors D05 — 5 doors Frozen and refrigerated cases, which are measured in doors rather than footage I Inches I037 — 37 inches Short sets and odd sections where feet would round away the detail Check the letter before you reach for the tape. A frozen set marked D05 doesn't want a measurement, it wants a door count — and someone who reads it as feet will conclude the section is wildly wrong and stop work over nothing. One thing to watch: D appears three times in the string and means something different each time. In D701 it's the division. In D03 it's the department. In the size field it's doors. Position tells you which — the size field is always the one just before the format code. Departments do change. Pet planograms recently moved from Department 01 to Department 03 following a family tree change. Older printouts and most people's memory still say 01. A department code that doesn't match what you expect isn't automatically a wrong planogram — check Part II, Commodities before you escalate it. Two more worth understanding: L00000 — all zeros. The location code. All zeros means this set is standard across stores , not built for one store in particular. A code with digits in it means the opposite, and that's worth noticing — a store-specific plan exists because that store needed something different. MX — the store format. Fred Meyer runs multiple formats, and a set built for one won't fit another. MX is the multi-department version covering both the grocery and home sides. If your footage or shelf count doesn't match, a format mismatch is one of the first things to check.

heading: 7.2 — The cover page tells you the job before you start
text: Page 1 carries the specs. Read them before you touch anything: Field This set Planogram Width 20 ft Planogram Height 78 inches Planogram Depth 22 inches Number of Shelves 30 Number of Products 339 Number of Pegs 0 Number of Bars 0 Effective Date 7/19/2026 Period Week P07 W01 Y2026 What this actually tells you: 20 feet of shelving, built as five 4-foot bays . Four feet is the standard bay width — you'll see it constantly. 30 shelves ÷ 5 bays = 6 shelves per bay . Zero pegs and zero bars means this is an all-shelf set. Nothing hangs. Effective Date is the date the set goes live in the store. It is not the date you work it, and it is not the date the file was created — this one was generated 6/9 for a set effective 7/19. Before you start, verify two things against the physical section: Measure the section. It should be 20 feet. Count the shelves. There should be 30. Either one off? Stop and contact me. Do not adjust the planogram to fit the shelf.

heading: 7.3 — Shelf heights, and the measurement that trips people up
text: Each bay lists its shelves with an exact height: Shelf Height from base shelf Shelf 1 0.00 — base shelf Shelf 2 13.00 in Shelf 3 25.00 in Shelf 4 37.00 in Shelf 5 49.00 in Shelf 6 61.00 in How to measure — this is the part people get wrong. The rule is printed directly on every page: the measurement is the distance from the top of one shelf to the top of the next shelf up. Top of shelf to top of shelf. Not top-of-shelf to the underside of the one above it. Those two methods differ by the thickness of the shelf itself, and if you use the wrong one across six shelves the whole bay drifts. Check your work: 61 inches to the top shelf, plus 11 inches of clearance above it, is the 72-inch fixture. Add the 6-inch base deck and you have the 78-inch planogram height off the floor. If your numbers close like that, you measured correctly. Three things that make the number right or wrong: Read the tape at eye level , straight on, the way you'd read a measuring cup. Looking down at the tape from above reads long. One shelf, it's nothing. Six shelves, the bay drifts. When the shelf won't sit at the exact height using the nearest hole in the gondola , leave too much space rather than too little. Too much and the product still fits. Too little and it doesn't go on the shelf at all. Bread and chips sit on wire shelves. Measure to where the product sits, not to the top of the front lip. The front edge of a wire shelf rides above its deck, and measuring to the lip puts every shelf above it too high. When the diagram and the table disagree, the table wins. The shelf-height list is the specification. The callouts along the left edge of the picture are a visual aid. The strip gives you a second opinion, and almost nobody uses it. Along the bottom of the shelf strip, printed in red in very small type, is DISTANCE FROM BASE SHELF and a number. That's how far that shelf sits above the base shelf. Use it. Measuring shelf to shelf up a bay means every measurement inherits the error in the one below it — six shelves, six chances to drift. The distance from the base shelf is taken from a single fixed datum, so it accumulates nothing. Set your heights the normal way, then check an upper shelf against its distance-from-base number. If those agree, everything underneath is right. Who makes these, and why your shelf doesn't always agree with them. Planograms are built by a central team — the Planogram Center of Excellence , PCOE . A separate team, LAMCOE , maps those planograms onto each store's floorplan. Between the two, every store gets told which plan goes on which fixture. That's why one plan covers a whole division, and why 7.6 exists. The plan is drawn to a standard. Your fixture is a real thing in a real building.

heading: 7.4 — Finding any product: Bay, Shelf, Position
text: Every item on the set has a three-part address, and it's how we'll talk about the work. Bay → Shelf → Position. Bay — which 4-foot section, numbered left to right, 1 through 5 Shelf — numbered bottom to top, 1 through 6 Position — left to right along that shelf, starting at 1 So "Bay 3, Shelf 5, Position 4" is one specific product, and there's no ambiguity about which one. The counting rules are exact, and two of them will catch you out. Bays Left to right across the planogram Shelves Bottom to top within each bay — and the count includes empty shelves and signage shelves. A shelf with nothing on it is still a shelf and still gets a number Shelf extenders Counted as the last fixture on the bay where the extender's left edge begins Positions Left to right. Start with the first item whose left edge falls inside the bay. Stop with the last item whose left edge falls inside the bay The empty and signage shelves rule is the one that bites. Section 8.2 has you count the shelves and confirm they match the planogram. Skip a signage shelf because it holds no product and your count is off by one — which reads as a planogram that doesn't fit your section, and sends you to your lead over nothing. The position start-and-stop rule is what resolves the straddling item. A product sitting across a bay seam belongs to whichever bay its left edge is in. That's why the same item appears in two bays' tables with the facings split between them. Positions run continuously across bay boundaries. You will see a bay's product table open with a row belonging to the previous bay — Bay 2's Shelf 6 list starts with an entry labeled Bay 1, Shelf 6, Position 17. That's a product physically straddling the seam between two bays. It's not an error. Set it once, from whichever bay you're working. On the diagram, a straddling product looks like a printing error. When an item lands right in the middle of a seam between two bays, there's no room to label it the usual way — so the planogram gives you a small arrow pointing at the seam, with the item information turned sideways and shrunk down to fit. It looks like something went wrong at the printer. It didn't. That sideways, tiny, arrowed label is the planogram telling you an item belongs right there, spanning the seam, with part of its facings on each side. When you see one, expect to find that same item listed in the position tables of both bays. This is also why a facing count can look wrong when it isn't — the planogram divides a product at the bay line and the shelf strip doesn't. Section 7.7 covers what to do about it.

heading: 7.5 — The position table, column by column
text: Column What it means Bay Which 4-ft section Fi... (Fixture) The shelf number Pos Position, left to right on that shelf UPC The barcode. This is the item's real identity — trust it over the description Fac Facings — how many of this product sit side by side across the front New/Chg Flags an item new to this set Product Description Abbreviated name Size Package size Height / Width Physical dimensions of the package Merch How it's merchandised — Unit or Display Safer Info Handling flags for regulated or hazardous items. Blank on this set — if it isn't blank on yours, ask me before handling On product descriptions: they're truncated and cryptic. HRB ES is Herbal Essences. TRSME is TreSemmé. GRNR FRC is Garnier Fructis. LORL is L'Oréal. AUSS is Aussie. You'll learn them fast, but when the description and the UPC disagree, scan the UPC. Descriptions repeat and mislead; UPCs don't.

heading: 7.6 — Facings
text: The Fac column is the number of that product across the front of the shelf, side by side. From Bay 1, Shelf 6 on this set: Pos Product Fac 1 HRB ES CURL BOOSTING MSSE 1 2 HRB ES TTL TWST CURL MSSE 2 3 H/ESS BDY ENVY VOLUM MOUS 1 4 HRB ES VOLUME HAIRSPRY 2 Position 2 gets two units across the front. Position 3 gets one. Get this wrong and the whole shelf shifts sideways, and every product to the right of your mistake lands in the wrong place. Facings are horizontal only. Fill the shelf front to back behind each facing as depth allows — this set is 22 inches deep. When the facings don't fit. Corporate issues one planogram for a set. There are close to 130 stores in this division and just about as many variations in how the shelving actually sits. The plan is drawn to a standard in an office; your section is a real fixture that's been rebuilt, bumped, and worked around for years. The two will not always agree, and that is ordinary — it is not a fault to report and wait on. Two rules cover nearly all of it: A product with multiple facings that won't all fit — take it down by one facing. Set the rest as planned. A product with no room for even one facing — look for a neighbor on the same shelf that has multiple facings, and take one from it. An item with one facing is on the shelf. An item with none is invisible to the customer and to the store's inventory. Both cases: call it out to your lead. Neither case stops your work. Keep setting. What does stop the work is a section that doesn't match at all — footage off, shelf count off, wrong version, wrong format. Facings that don't quite fit are a fitting problem, and you solve those on the shelf. A section that isn't the right size is a planning problem, and that's the one worth stopping for.

heading: 7.7 — The shelf strip
text: GoGo squeeZ variety-pack boxes on shelf — an example of product whose shelf-strip facing count may span multiple bays. Shelf strip with size codes — the letter-number pairs identify which tag size to use. Another shelf-strip example with height and width codes for tag sizing. The planogram is what you carry. The shelf strip is what stays on the shelf , and it repeats the same instructions in a form you can read while your hands are full. The strip slides into the data skin along the front edge. The header band runs along the top and tells you where you are: On the header What it tells you Bay ## Shelf ## The bay and fixture this strip belongs to POG space station name The full planogram code — the same string as the file name in 7.1 Period, week, year Written like P4 Wk2 Y21 . When this plan takes effect Division and store number Which division and which store Aisle number and orientation Which aisle, and which side of it you're standing at Generic POG description The plain-language name of the set Each product entry on the strip carries: On the entry What it tells you Commodity number The commodity this item belongs to UPC and barcode The item's real identity. Scan this, not the description Product description and size Abbreviated name and pack size Wholesaler name Who supplies it Black lines The position boundaries. Product sits between the lines C / H / W The stack notation — see below SRP Marked in green. Leave the product in its shipping tray or box ⇔ The commodity spans bays. See below DISTANCE FROM BASE SHELF Red, small type. The shelf's height above the base shelf — see 7.3 DSL tag size Which size digital label this position takes — DSL stores only Small item strips — spices, extracts, anything narrow — carry the same information in a compressed layout. Same fields, less room. The ⇔ symbol means the item spans bays. It's the printed version of everything 7.4 describes, and it's the fastest way to tell a straddling item from a mistake — the strip is telling you outright. It continues onto the same shelf in the next bay. Each bay has its own shelves, so physically it's a different piece of steel — but it's the same shelf number, the same height, the same horizontal row. Bay 2 Shelf 3 carries on as Bay 3 Shelf 3. Look sideways, never up or down. A spanning item stays in the horizontal flow with the products beside it. The facing count on the strip is the total across both bays , not the part in front of you. So a strip reading W3 against a Fac column reading 2 means one more facing is waiting at the start of the next bay, on that same shelf. Go and find it before you decide the numbers are wrong. The stack notation: C, H, W. Letter Officially On the shelf C Capping Number of caps — units laid flat on top of the standing product H High Number of layers — how many the product stacks upward W Wide Number of rows — the facings, same as the Fac column The official words are Capping, High, and Wide. Most people say caps, layers, and facings. Both are correct and you'll hear both. When W and the planogram's Fac column disagree, check the adjoining bay first. Most of the time they aren't actually disagreeing. Here's why. The planogram is written bay by bay. The strip runs the full length of the run. So a product sitting at the end of a shelf often continues as position 1 on the same shelf in the next bay over. The planogram splits it — 2 facings in this bay's table, 1 more in the next bay's — while the strip, which doesn't care where the bays divide, shows all 3. So a strip reading W3 against a Fac column reading 2 usually means there's one more facing of that item waiting at the start of the next bay. Add the two together before you treat it as a conflict. If you check the same shelf in the adjoining bay and it genuinely isn't that, follow the strip — if there's room for it. If there isn't, you're back to 7.6 : take it down a facing and keep setting. Either way, tell your lead. Neither one stops the work. SRP is the one that catches people. On a strip or a planogram it means Shelf Ready Packaging — the product stays on the shelf in the tray or box it shipped in, not unpacked. Canned vegetables, baby food, frozen vegetables. In a conversation about pricing the same three letters mean Suggested Retail Price. If you're reading it off a strip, it's the packaging one.

heading: 7.8 — Unit vs. Display
text: The Merch column tells you how the item is presented. Unit — normal shelf placement, standing as the product is designed to stand. Display — the item sits in or on a display piece, often a small tray or riser . On this set, five TreSemmé items on Bay 1 Shelf 5 are marked Display. If a Display item arrives without its display piece, don't improvise a substitute. Ask me.

heading: 7.9 — The NEW and DELETE pages
text: Page 2 of every planogram lists what's changing: Products Added To Planogram (NEW) — items joining the set. This set adds 12. Products Removed From Planogram (DELETE) — items leaving. This set drops 7. New items are also flagged inline in the position tables, so you'll see them twice. A trap worth knowing: the same UPC can appear on both lists. On this set, LORL STDLN CLEAN GEL (UPC 0007124911933) is listed as added and as removed. That normally means the item is moving — different bay, different shelf, or different facing count — not that it's leaving the store. Set it where the position table puts it, and don't box it as discontinued because you saw it on the delete list. When in doubt about a product on both lists, ask me before you pull it.

heading: 7.10 — Fixtures that aren't shelves
text: Most of what you'll set is shelves. When it isn't, the counting changes — and if you assume shelf rules on a table or a chest , the addresses won't line up. Tables — bakery display tables, produce tables Each planogram is one bay Fixtures count front to back , from the front of the store backward Positions count left to right, then front to back within the table On a layout, tables are shaded differently from each other so they stay distinguishable in grayscale print Pegboards An open pegboard — no rods or bars — counts as one fixture , holding all the product pegged to it A pegboard behind shelves is sequenced by its topmost position. A board between shelves 4 and 6 takes position 1 A pegboard with no product positions isn't counted at all Each bar or rod counts as one fixture if it holds a position or a sign. Empty bars and rods aren't counted Positions on rods and bars count left to right Positions on an open pegboard count top to bottom, then left to right . Products differing in height by a couple of inches count as the same row Chests — bunkers and open freezer wells A chest may be one bay , or several counted left to right Bins and trays count left to right, then front to back Positions count left to right, then front to back , within the tray or within the bay if there are no trays Sub-fixtures A sub-fixture is a fixture sitting inside another fixture. It inherits the parent's number and gets a three- or four-digit code: the first one or two digits are the parent, the rest is the sub-fixture counted bottom to top. Code Reads as 203 Third sub-fixture on fixture 2 401 First sub-fixture on fixture 4 1002 Second sub-fixture on fixture 10 Positions inside a sub-fixture count left to right, then front to back.

heading: 7.11 — Working the set
text: Put it together in this order: Confirm the effective date matches the set you were assigned Measure the section — 20 ft — and count the shelves — 30 Work bay by bay, left to right Within each bay, work bottom shelf to top Within each shelf, work left to right by position Set facings exactly as the Fac column reads Tag the set — paper tags to the left of each product, or digital labels installed and associated. Section 8 , Step 8 has both Bottom to top, left to right, one bay at a time. That order is not a preference — it's what keeps you from rebuilding a shelf you already finished.

heading: Section 8 — Performing a Full Reset
text: Section 8 — Performing a Full Reset A full reset rebuilds an entire category to a new planogram. Everything comes off, the shelves get reconfigured, and the category goes back up to the new plan. This section teaches the full reset end to end. Partial projects — NIIs and maintenances — are the same work applied to part of a set, and Section 8.6 covers what changes. Settle this first Does this store have digital shelf labels? Look at the shelf edge. Paper price tags, or small digital screens? Everything in this section is the same either way until Step 8, where the two split. Fred Meyer is partway through the rollout, so both kinds of store are live right now, and you can't assume from one visit to the next.

heading: 8.1 — Rules that apply the entire time
text: The aisle stays shoppable. Customers are shopping around you for the whole project. Keep your materials, baskets, and carts on one side so there's always a clear path through. This is not a courtesy — an aisle you've blocked is an aisle the store can't sell from. Where you can, work a bay at a time rather than opening the whole set at once. One cart in the aisle per person working. Two of you resetting cookies with four carts pulled means two carts in the aisle and two parked out of the way. Carts multiply faster than people do, and a cart nobody is standing at is just an obstacle. Shopping carts are ours to use, and only ours. Store policy is that vendors don't use shopping carts. Retail Odyssey has been granted an exception by Kroger corporate specifically for resets, so you are allowed. Expect occasional pushback from store associates who haven't heard about the exception — be polite, and tell your lead rather than arguing it out. Two things make the exception stick: never leave product sitting in a cart in the back room , and empty every cart and return it to the corral before you leave. The planogram is the authority — but the shelf is real. You set what the plan says, where it says, in the quantity it says. Where the fixture won't take it, you adjust facings on the shelf and call it out rather than stopping. Section 7.6 has the rule. What you don't do is redesign the set. Know which kind of mismatch you have. Footage off, shelf count off, wrong version or format — that's a planning problem, and you stop before you dismantle anything. Product that won't quite fit the facings it's given — that's a fitting problem, and you solve it and keep moving. Standing rule Refrigerated and frozen product gets 20 minutes out of the case. Longer than that and it goes into the walk-in cooler or freezer. Watch which one — refrigerated product in a freezer is a loss, and so is the reverse. Exception Bakery is 15 minutes, not 20. Bakery product is delicate and melts fast. See Part II, Bakery .

heading: 8.2 — Before you touch product
text: Work through this in order. Each step catches a problem that gets more expensive the longer it goes unnoticed. Pull your materials from the Kompass cart — Kompass Notes , planogram, strips, and tags Check the planogram version and effective date against what your lead is working from Read the Kompass Notes for this project — they tell you what's discontinued and flag any known discrepancies Confirm the section size matches the planogram — feet, doors, or inches, depending on what the plan calls for. Check the letter on the size code before you measure; a frozen set is counted in doors, not feet. Section 7.1 Count the shelves and confirm they match the planogram Check whether new shelves have been supplied. If new shelving is available for this set, it goes in — old shelves get swapped, not reused Count your strips against the planogram. Do this before anything comes off the shelf — see below Stage your boxes — labeled and ready before anything comes off the shelf Locate the new-item stock in the back room so you're not hunting for it mid-set DSL stores only: confirm you have a Zebra . Leads, please ask the store for it early, before the shift starts. No Zebra by mid-shift, escalate to me — don't wait it out. I provide the login Stop Footage or shelf count doesn't match? Stop. Tell your lead before you dismantle anything. A wrong planogram caught now costs five minutes; caught halfway through a teardown, it costs the afternoon. The set size gets written down and stuck to the first bay before anything comes off the shelf. Confirm it against the planogram here, not later. Same note, close up. This is the number every shelf height and facing count depends on. Where the planogram states the set size. Check the letter on the size code before you measure — Section 7.1. The same fields, enlarged. Feet, doors, or inches depends on what the plan calls for.

heading: Count the strips before you pull a single one
text: This is the check people skip, and it's the one that leaves a set unfinishable. Full reset: you should have a strip for every position on the planogram. Short by any, tell your lead before you start Partial or NII: expect strips only for what's changing. That's normal and correct — but it means you pull only the strips you have replacements for The trap is on partials. The packet arrives with the planogram and a partial set of strips, which looks complete because a planogram came with it. Strip the whole set on that assumption and you've got positions with nothing to put back — and no way to fix it until another packet arrives. Match strips to positions first. Pull second.

heading: 8.3 — The working order
text: Three nested rules, and they never change: Bay by bay , left to right — Bay 1 through Bay 5 Within a bay, bottom shelf to top — Shelf 1 upward Within a shelf, position 1 outward — left to right Bottom to top matters more than it sounds. Product set on a higher shelf gets disturbed every time you adjust something below it. Working upward means you never rebuild the same shelf twice. If the set has both shelves and pegs, set the shelves bottom-up first, then hang the pegs top-down. Hanging pegs before the shelves are set means reaching over finished product, and something always comes off the hook. Complete one shelf before starting the next. To keep product off the floor, park items temporarily in open slots on shelves you haven't reached yet.

heading: Step 1 — Pull discontinued items
text: Before the teardown, clear out what's leaving. Work from the Kompass Notes — they designate the DIs for this project DIs carry closeout tags on the shelf edge; that's how you spot them Route them to the store associate, or place them in clearly labeled boxes Pull the tags with the items and keep them together You'll also find items the Notes don't list — damaged product, out-of-code product, and items not in the set at all. Those come off too, into their own labeled boxes. Part II covers the pull categories and where each one goes. Never take product home with you. Not damaged, not discontinued, not out of code. It goes to the store for disposition. This sounds obvious right up until someone hands you a dented box and says "just take it."

heading: Step 2 — Strip what has to move, and clean it
text: You don't empty the whole set. You empty what has to move. A shelf whose product isn't changing position and whose height isn't changing doesn't come off. Stripping it anyway costs you the time to take it down and put it back, and every handling is a chance to damage something or set it back wrong. Strip a shelf when: The shelf height is changing Product on it is moving position, or coming off the set The shelf itself is being swapped for a new one The shelf edge needs work — rail, channel, or strip being replaced Leave it when none of those apply. Same principle as 8.6: touch what changed. The DSL guidance says the same thing about tags — slide and re-associate rather than pulling the lot off. Product, tags, strips: on this job the instinct is always to move what moves and leave the rest alone. When you do strip a shelf: The tag travels with the product. Pull the tag with its item and stick it to the last piece of that product in the cart. Whoever sets it back then has a tag in hand the moment they pick that item up Load the cart from the handle end , left to right, snaked up to the top, like items touching. If you walk away, the next person can pick up exactly where you stopped without guessing Wipe down the shelf and the tag molding with the cleaning supplies from the Kompass cart New shelves get cleaned too if they've been sitting in storage Clean every shelf you moved, and its molding — not just the ones that looked dirty. You won't have a better opportunity, because that shelf is never emptier than it is right now. A shelf you didn't need to strip doesn't need cleaning either.

heading: Step 3 — Set the shelf height
text: Read the height for this shelf from the planogram's position table Measure from the top of the shelf to the top of the next shelf up — the rule is printed on every planogram page Read the tape at eye level , head-on, the way you'd read a measuring cup. Looking down at it from an angle reads long, and across six shelves that drift adds up If the shelf won't sit at the exact height using the nearest hole, leave too much space rather than too little. Too little and the product doesn't fit at all Bread and chips sit on wire shelves — measure to where the product sits, not to the top of the front lip. The front edge of a wire shelf is not its deck Adjust the lowest shelf first if it needs to move, then work upward Move a single shelf yourself. Anything deeper than 15 inches takes two people , and steel beams, wood shelves, and shelving structures always take help If your heights close correctly against the fixture height, you measured right. Section 7.3 walks through that check.

heading: Step 4 — Set the shelf edge
text: Shelf-edge hardware goes in with the shelf empty. It's far harder once product is in front of you. Every store: Check the data skins . They're the clear channel guides snapped to the front edge. Damaged, missing, or wrong size, tell your lead — a strip has nowhere to go without one Pull the existing strips — but only the ones you have replacements for. You counted them in 8.2 Install the new strips per the planogram. The planogram is what tells you which strip goes where — the Kompass Notes tell you what's changing, not where the strips land DSL stores, one addition. The shelf edge carries an ESL rail , and the channel snaps into it. Check the rail before the strip goes in — a bent or missing rail means the tag has nowhere to sit. The parts reference in Part II will tell you which one you need and how to ask for it. Order of assembly Rail, then channel or data strip, then planogram strip, then tag. Never a tag before a strip. The tag gets matched to the strip during association, so a tag installed first has nothing to match to and comes back off. The channel data strips still have the slot behind them for the travel strip to slide into. Nothing changes about how you handle travel strips in a DSL store. A full reset replaces every strip on the set.

heading: Step 5 — Set the category to the planogram
text: Place each product at its position on the shelf, working left to right Set the facing count exactly as the Fac column reads — the number of that product side by side across the front Align product between the black lines on the strip. Those lines are the position boundaries All labels face forward Fill front to back behind each facing as depth allows When the product description and the UPC disagree, scan the UPC. Descriptions are abbreviated and repeat across similar items When the strip's facing count doesn't match the planogram's, look one bay over. The planogram is written bay by bay; the strip runs the full length of the run. A product at the end of a shelf usually continues into the next bay, and the strip is showing you the combined total. Section 7.7 has the detail If the facings don't fit, take the product down by one facing and keep setting. No room for even one facing, borrow a facing from a neighbor on the same shelf that has several, so the item still lands somewhere. Tell your lead either way — but don't stop the set over it. Section 7.6 covers both cases. If a product isn't in stock, hold its space with a dummy facing — a same-size item turned backwards in the slot. Backwards is the point: nobody buys it by mistake, the gap stays the right width, and whoever fills it later doesn't have to re-measure. Tell your lead so the store knows there's a hole. Get a facing count wrong and everything to the right of it lands in the wrong place. Verify as you go rather than at the end.

heading: Step 6 — Rotate the stock
text: Older product to the front, newer product to the back of each facing. This is proper Key Retailing rotation and it applies to every facing you set. It's the step most often skipped, and it matters: product left sitting behind newer stock ages out and becomes a write-off for the store. A shelf that's perfectly set with reversed rotation is a shelf that generates out-of-code product in a few weeks — and it will look correct to anyone walking it.

heading: Step 7 — Bring up the new-item stock
text: Pull all new-item stock from the back room onto the shelf New items are flagged in the planogram's position tables and listed on the planogram's NEW page Perishable and frozen new items have a designated location — if it came out of a fridge or freezer, it goes back into one

heading: Step 8 — Tag the set
text: This is where the two kinds of store split. Look at the shelf edge and pick the path. One rule applies in both, so learn it once. If a position has no tag: Check for a shelf strip. If there's a strip, the strip stands in. Don't hand-write anything and don't improvise a replacement Highlight that position on the planogram Give the planogram to your lead , who passes it to the store's price changer Where a set runs without strips at all, hand-write a tag so the product isn't sitting unlabeled — then highlight and hand it up the same way. What you never do is leave a position with nothing on it and say nothing about it. A highlighted planogram is how the store finds out; your memory at the end of a shift is not.

heading: 8A — Paper tag stores
text: Tags come from the store's price changer , staged ahead of the visit. Some stores call the same person the scan or pricing coordinator Place each tag to the left of its product Hang every tag provided Missing a tag? Follow the rule above — strip stands in, highlight the planogram, hand it to your lead

heading: 8B — Digital shelf label stores
text: In a DSL store the digital label replaces the paper tag. You are not hanging both. Where DSL goes Center Store grocery Checklanes Coolers — magnet mount Parts of produce, not all of it Where it does not currently go Freezers · Frozen · General Merchandise · Floral · Service Departments · Fuel Center · Freestanding Displays · Wine · Tobacco · Seasonal · American Greetings · Gift Cards · Clip Strips · Lobby · Dump Bins · Furniture General Merchandise stays on UPLs and is worked as normal. Paper tags, no change. This list is current, not permanent. Check with your lead if you're unsure. Pick the right size — the number is printed on the shelf strip. Size Where 1.5 The smallest tag. Tight barcode space 2.6 The majority size throughout the store 4.2 / 4.5 Large format. Produce bins and similar fixtures Magnets Coolers only. No magnet available, use the magnetic adapter or the alternative in the parts reference Match the tag to the number on the strip. If it covers another barcode, size DOWN. A label that hides a barcode stops the shelf being scannable, which defeats the point of having it. Associating a tag Open the DSL app — Assign DSL / Match DSL Scan the DSL tag. The clicker at the bottom right fires the beam Scan the shelf strip barcode , or the product Watch for the flash. That's what confirms the link Snap the tag into place , then move on Scan the DSL first, then the barcode. That order is what links them. Take the old paper tag down only after the screen has flashed. Not before. If the association fails and you've already pulled the paper, the position has nothing on it at all. Snapping it in. Go in from the bottom — pop the tag toward the top, then pop the bottom in. There are clips along the bottom edge, and the snap is loud and obvious when it seats correctly. If you didn't hear it, it isn't in. Holders you'll meet: J-2 skins, which are clip-on; the dairy, meat and dry holder that turns up across most of those sets; and the produce holder. Part II has the full parts reference. When product moves Move the tag with the product Tags from confirmed deletes can be reused for new items No tags left on empty spaces Don't do this Don't strip a whole set of tags and re-hang them. Slide the tag to where it now belongs and re-associate it to the product that's there. You don't have to take a tag off the rail to change what it's pointing at, and you don't have to disassociate it first — just associate it to the new product. Pulling every tag off a set and starting again is hours of work to reach the same place. It also puts a pile of loose tags on your cart, and loose tags are how deletes end up un-disassociated. Disassociating You do not have to disassociate a tag before associating a new one. Skip straight to associating. What must be disassociated is every tag from a delete, at end of set. Open the app, select Disassociate, scan the tag, confirm. Unused tags go back on the Kompass cart . Leftovers break re-association. A tag that's still associated to something deleted can't be cleanly picked up by the next set. This is the reason the end-of-set sweep isn't optional. Removal tools Removal tools live on the Kompass cart. They're ours, not the store's — don't leave them behind. Tags come off without tools and won't break. A putty knife or a canoe-clip tool works; the flat edge is what matters. If you can't get a Zebra Your supervisor provides the login. The login is tied to the store — there's no store to select , and multiple team leads can be logged in at different stores at the same time. Leads: request the Zebra from the store early AM, before the shift starts. No Zebra by mid-shift, escalate the same day. Don't argue with the store — escalation handles it. Escalation path Team Lead reports immediately → me → Kompass Manager.

heading: Step 9 — Verify
text: Before you call the shelf done: Every tag matched to the product it belongs to Facing counts match the Fac column Shelf heights match the planogram Rotation is correct — older forward Labels facing forward, product aligned between the strip's black lines Nothing from the pull categories is still sitting on the shelf DSL stores, four more: Correct tag size on every position Tags moved with their product Every delete disassociated Unused tags back on the Kompass cart — along with the removal tools Worth knowing: finished sets get checked against the planogram by Store Intelligence , which pairs AI with our planograms to confirm the set matches the plan.
