A set that looks finished but isn't will get flagged after you've left. Verifying now is faster than coming back.

heading: Step 10 — Close out the set
text: DSL stores: every delete disassociated, every unused tag and removal tool back on the Kompass cart. Leftovers break re-association for whoever works this set next, and the removal tools are ours Move backstock to the designated store associate, or into labeled overstock boxes Clear the area of clutter and trash Return boxes, crates, and any borrowed equipment to the store receiver Empty and return every shopping cart to the corral Leave the aisle better than you found it

heading: 8.5 — Where the mistakes happen
text: Mistake What it costs Setting from the description instead of the UPC Wrong product in the slot, often not caught until the walk-through Measuring shelf-top to shelf-bottom Every height off by the thickness of a shelf, compounding up the bay Facing count off by one Everything to the right of it shifts out of position Reversed rotation Invisible on the walk-through, generates out-of-code product weeks later Setting top-down instead of bottom-up Rebuilding shelves you already finished Installing strips after setting product Slow, awkward, and you'll knock product loose Installing a DSL tag before the strip Nothing to associate it to — the tag comes back off Leaving an active tag on an empty space The shelf advertises a price for a product that isn't there Tearing down before verifying footage The most expensive mistake on this list

heading: 8.6 — What changes on a Partial
text: NIIs and maintenances use the same mechanics on part of a set. The discipline is restraint — you touch what changed and nothing else. Step Full Reset Partial Discontinued items Pull all DIs per the Notes Same Strips Replace every strip on the set — confirm you have a full set first You'll get strips only for what's changing. Pull only what you can replace Setting Set the entire category to the new planogram Set only the changing area to the new strips No strips in the category — Cut the new items into the set per the planogram Stripping Strip only the shelves that have to move Same — and far fewer of them Cleaning Wipe all moved shelving and tag moldings Wipe only the affected shelves Tags — paper Hang all provided, hand-write as needed Same Tags — DSL Tag and associate the whole set Tag and associate the changed positions ; disassociate anything removed Backstock To the associate or labeled boxes Same Aisle Shoppable throughout Same The temptation on a partial is to tidy up neighboring shelves while you're there. Don't. Work outside the changing area isn't tracked, isn't signed off, and can put a shelf out of sync with a planogram someone else is working from.

heading: 8.7 — Departments that work differently
text: Bakery runs its own version of a Kompass reset — a different way of reading the planogram, black ID tags under product, magnetic shelf strips, POG books on clear hooks, and a separate completion standard. Read the bakery section in Part II before your first bakery reset. Don't work one off this section alone.

heading: Section 9 — Closing Out
text: Section 9 — Closing Out Section 8 tells you how to close out a set . This section is about closing out the shift — the last thirty minutes, when the work is done and it would be easy to leave a store that looks like a reset happened in it. That last part matters more than it sounds. The store team sees the aisle after you're gone, and they form their whole opinion of us from it. A perfect set in a wrecked aisle reads as a bad visit.

heading: 9.1 — Walk the set
text: Every set gets walked before it's called done. This one has no exceptions. Who you walk it with depends on your role: You walk with Rep Your lead Lead The store Walk it before you clean up , while everything is still out and fixable. This is the cheapest correction in the whole process — a facing count spotted in thirty seconds costs two minutes to fix with the cart still beside you, and a return trip if it's found after you've gone. There's a reason it's someone else's eyes. By the time you finish a set you can't see it fresh any more. You've looked at it for an hour, you know what you intended, and you'll read the shelf as the thing you meant to build. Somebody walking up cold sees what's actually there. Reps: have the planogram in your hand when your lead walks up. Your lead will check the things Section 8 's verify step lists. Leads: walking the completed work with the store is how the visit closes. It's also where anything that couldn't be finished gets said out loud rather than discovered later. If you highlighted anything on the planogram — a position you couldn't tag , a facing you had to reduce — hand it over on the walk and say what you did. Section 8 , Step 8.

heading: 9.2 — Clear the aisle
text: Nothing you brought in stays in the aisle. Not a cart, not a tote, not a bread tray, not a milk crate, not an empty box you meant to come back for. Work through this: Carts, totes, trays, and crates out of the aisle entirely Product from the pull categories delivered where it goes — damaged and out-of-date to the receiver, backstock to the store associate or into labeled boxes, not-in-set product routed per your lead Trash, cardboard, and plastic disposed of properly. Cardboard goes to the baler area — you do not operate the baler unless you're 18 or over and someone has shown you that specific machine Spills swept or cleaned , including the ones that were there when you arrived What you worked, conditioned to standard. On a full reset that's the entire set. On an NII or a partial, it's the area you worked — see Part II, Conditioning by Department On scope: a partial may be allocated fifteen minutes, and conditioning a whole aisle isn't inside fifteen minutes. Condition what you were sent to do, and do it properly, rather than spreading thin across work that isn't yours.

heading: 9.3 — Return what isn't yours
text: Borrowed equipment back to the receiver — hand trucks, dollies, U-boats, step ladders Shopping carts emptied and returned to the corral. Every one. The cart exception in Section 8.1 holds because we return them; it stops holding the first time a team leaves six carts in an aisle overnight Your personal items collected from wherever your lead designated at the start of the shift Nothing of the store's goes home with you — not damaged product , not discontinued product, not an empty display piece. Section 8 , Step 1

heading: 9.4 — Sign-off
text: You don't touch the sign-off paperwork. That's your lead's job everywhere, without exception. You should still understand how it works, because the quality of what you hand your lead determines how quickly it goes. Photographing your completed work is different. Some districts have the rep photograph their own sets; others have the lead do it. Your lead will tell you which applies to you — ask on your first shift rather than assuming. If it's you, 9.5 is the standard. How the work gets signed out: Fred Meyer signs off on completed Kompass work Two methods are in use right now — fax and photo. Which one applies depends on the store and the project. Your lead will know; if you're the lead and you don't, ask me The store's sign-off is usually coordinated by the Kompass Champion , though that role is rarely staffed anymore. In practice most of the coordination falls to your lead What we do not do: CAO and Kompass Completion are Fred Meyer systems. We have no logins for them, and we are not permitted to sign work out in them. If anyone in a store asks you to complete work in either system, the answer is no, and you tell your lead. This isn't a preference — it's the boundary between our work and theirs, and crossing it creates a record nobody can defend. Ratings and the store visit summary still exist in the process. They aren't heavily used at the moment, and where they are, they're the manager's step rather than something you fill in.

heading: 9.5 — Photographing completed work
text: Correct after-photo framing — vertical lines bound the bay, horizontal lines align to shelf edges, and the arrow marks the capture width. If photographing your sets is part of your role, you'll be set up with a Store Intelligence login and you submit the photos yourself, directly in the app. Ask me if you don't have one. Check which instance you're logged into. The app serves more than one program, and each one has its own instance. Instance Who kroger Fred Meyer Kompass teams — this is you krogerdc The Display Compliance scan team — different job, different team Make sure you're in kroger before you submit anything. Work submitted to the wrong instance isn't recorded against your reset, and you won't get the feedback that tells you what still needs addressing. Photograph after your lead has checked the set , not before. Shoot it first and you're photographing a section that's about to change. The photo is the record. A blurry or badly framed image doesn't just look sloppy — it can't be read, so the work it documents may as well not have been done. The capture order is the same order you set the shelf: start at Bay 1 and work left to right. One bay per photo. Every bay gets its own image, no matter how big or small the section is. Don't try to fit two bays in a frame and don't shoot a whole run at once. Four requirements on every shot: Angle Stand directly in front of the middle of the bay and hold the camera square to the section, both vertically and horizontally. Shooting from an angle distorts product size from top to bottom and left to right, which is exactly the thing the photo is meant to show accurately Full section Every product and every shelf edge visible. Top items complete — not clipped , bottom shelf in frame, and the shelf breaks at both sides captured Clarity Sharp and in focus. No blur, no glare Glass doors Open the doors first, then shoot. Glass gives you reflection and distortion, and neither can be corrected afterwards Nothing in the way. No carts, no ladders, no shadow falling across the product, no teammate in frame. Move it and take the shot. Before you move to the next bay, ask yourself four questions: Am I standing square to the middle of the bay? Can I see every product and every shelf edge, top to bottom? Is the image sharp — no blur, no glare, nothing blocking the shelf? Did I start at Bay 1 and work left to right? Check it on the spot. You're standing in front of the set right now, and you won't be in an hour. Submit in the app, then read what it gives you back. Store Intelligence doesn't just store the photo. It tells you what needs addressing — a facing that doesn't match the plan, a position that reads wrong, a gap it can see. That comes back to you while you're still in the aisle. Fix what it flags before you move on. That's the whole point of submitting from the floor rather than from the parking lot. Then re-shoot the bay so the record matches the corrected set. This is the loop: Set the bay → lead checks it → photograph it → submit → fix what comes back → re-shoot A bay that comes out clean is finished. Move to the next one.

heading: 9.6 — What happens after you leave
text: Your set doesn't stop being looked at when you walk out. Store Intelligence keeps working after the shift. If you submitted your own photos, you've already seen most of what it has to say and fixed it in the aisle — that's 9.5 . Where the lead shoots instead, or where something surfaces later, the flag comes back to the team that worked the set rather than to the person standing in front of it. Either way, the fix is the same and it's cheaper the earlier it happens: two minutes in the aisle, a phone call the next day, or a return trip. Neither of these is a reason to be nervous. They're a reason to spend the extra two minutes in 9.1 while the cart is still beside you.

heading: 9.7 — Clocking out
text: Clock out in the Field App at the end of your shift, not in the aisle at the end of your last set. Section 3.4 covers the timing — you check the app before and after, not during. Confirm your hours the same day. A missed punch is easy to fix on the day it happens and increasingly annoying afterwards.

heading: 9.8 — When the work isn't finished
text: Sometimes a project doesn't close. A section wasn't ready, product didn't arrive, a planogram didn't match and the resolution didn't come back in time. Tell your lead before you leave, not after. What your lead needs to know: What's done and what isn't Exactly where you stopped — bay, shelf, position What's blocking it Where the materials and the pulled product are An unfinished set that's documented is a scheduling problem. An unfinished set nobody mentioned is a surprise for whoever opens that aisle tomorrow, and it costs three times as much to pick up. Leave it clean either way. Unfinished is not the same as abandoned — 9.2 and 9.3 still apply.

text: Multiple facings won't all fit Take it down by one facing . Keep working No room for even one facing Borrow a facing from a neighbor with several. Keep working Footage, shelf count, version or format wrong Stop. Tell your lead Both fitting cases: call it out to your lead. Neither stops the set. Product not in stock: dummy facing — same-size item turned backwards . Bakery is the exception: the facing stays blank.

heading: Tagging — 8.4 Step 8
text: No tag on a position? Strip present → the strip stands in. No strip → hand-write one. Either way: highlight it on the planogram and hand the planogram to your lead.

text: Order: rail → channel → strip → tag. Never a tag before a strip. Size Where 1.5 Tight barcode space 2.6 Most of the store 4.2 / 4.5 Produce bins, large format Magnet Coolers only Size is printed on the strip. Covers another barcode → size DOWN. Leftovers break re-association. Unused tags and removal tools back on the Kompass cart . Not currently installed in: freezers, frozen, GM, floral, service departments, fuel center, freestanding displays, wine, tobacco, seasonal , American Greetings, gift cards, clip strips, lobby, dump bins, furniture. GM stays on UPLs.

heading: The five box labels — Part II, Storage
text: Backstock · Discontinued · Not In Set · Damaged · Expired Sort into them as you pull and the labeling takes care of itself. Label as you fill, not at the end. Boxed product: leave it with the receiver if they can take it soon. If not, palletize it.

heading: Cold product
text: 20 minutes out of the case. Bakery is 15. Watch which one you put it back in — refrigerated into a freezer is a write-off, and so is the reverse.

heading: Before you leave — Section 9
text: Walk the set. Rep → with your lead. Lead → with the store. Aisle clear — no carts, totes, trays, crates Pull categories delivered, trash gone, spills cleaned What you worked, conditioned. Full reset : the whole set. Partial: your area Every cart emptied and returned to the corral Borrowed equipment back to the receiver After photos, submitted in Store Intelligence — fix what it flags before you move on Clock out in the Field App Can't finish? Tell your lead before you leave. What's done, exactly where you stopped, what's blocking it, where the materials are.

heading: Who to ask for what
text: Team Lead Anything on the day. First stop, always Me Anything your lead can't resolve. Logins, missing channels, escalations Price changer Tags and pricing. Via your lead Receiver U-boats, ladders, boxed product, damaged and out-of-date Bakery team Where deletes go, where new product is File Maintenance Coordinator Black ID tags Escalation: Team Lead → me → Kompass Manager.

heading: Things that are always true
text: The planogram is the authority. The shelf is real. Adjust facings, never redesign the set Scan the UPC , not the description Strip only what has to move. Height changing, product moving, shelf swapped, shelf edge being worked — otherwise leave it The tag travels with the product Older to the front, newer to the back A loose shelf is in your hands or locked into the gondola . There is no third state Nothing goes home with you 18 or older, and shown that machine, before you touch a baler

heading: Part II — Aisle Navigation
text: Part II — Aisle Navigation Two kinds of sign tell you where things are. Aisle markers hang over the aisle. Outriggers stick out from the gondola . Between them, they'll take you from the front of the store to the eight feet you've been assigned. Learning to read them is the fastest way to stop needing directions.

heading: Aisle markers
text: Overhead aisle marker showing the aisle number and category list for shoppers. Aisle 19 marker in the beverage section — category names printed on the hanging sign panels. The aisle marker hangs over the aisle and lists the commodities in it. Two styles of sign, read the same way.

heading: The order is a size ranking
text: The commodities listed are the ones with the most footage in that aisle, arranged largest to smallest. So the first thing on the sign is the biggest commodity down there — not the most important one, and not the one nearest the front. Read it that way and you can tell how an aisle is weighted before you walk into it. Commodities too small to earn a place aren't listed at all. An aisle contains more than its sign says.

heading: Reading order
text: Style Read it Two-column — inserts side by side Top left, top right, then down a row and left to right again. A single insert on the bottom row sits centered Single-column — a vertical list Straight down from the top

heading: Conventional and natural
text: Two inserts that look like the same commodity — candy and natural candy — are conventional and Natural Foods listed separately. They sit side by side , or on a vertical sign, conventional first with natural directly below it. Conventional gets listed first and natural is added where there's room, so a natural insert on the sign means that aisle carries enough natural product in that commodity to be worth calling out.

heading: Blanks
text: A blank is a filler panel in a slot with no verbiage on it. It means the sign is complete and that slot was spare. It doesn't mean anything is missing.

heading: Outriggers
text: An outrigger sign mounted over a gondola run — the sign text identifies the category above the shelf. Paired outrigger signs in the health and wellness aisle identifying adjacent subcategories. Refrigerated-aisle outriggers with English and Spanish category labels over reach-in cooler doors. Aisle-number sign combined with category outriggers over a vitamin and supplement set. Outriggers mount to the gondola and mark individual sets within the aisle. The aisle marker gets you to the right aisle; the outrigger gets you to the right eight feet of it. When your Kompass Notes name a commodity, the outrigger is what you're scanning for as you walk. Style Where you'll see it Standard Grocery, household, GM T-bracket HBC and OTC KPNR HBC and OTC . Inserts slide into wood sign holders. An older style, still in plenty of stores Case outriggers Refrigerated and frozen cases. Mounted either by screws or by magnet

heading: Aisle sequence
text: Sequence is the order sets are laid out along the aisle. Your planogram sits in that order. This is the useful one when something looks wrong. A set that appears to be in the wrong place is usually a sequence question, not a planogram error — the aisle is laid out to a plan, and the markers and outriggers were built from that same plan. The store-layout term for the same idea is adjacency : how sets sit next to each other along the run .

heading: Part II — Bakery
text: Part II — Bakery Read this before your first bakery reset , and keep it with you on visit day. Bakery is a Kompass reset like any other, and almost none of the mechanics are the same. What's different: The planogram is read differently , and it lives on the table rather than in your hand Black ID tags go under the product instead of shelf strips in front of it Magnetic shelf strip on most refrigerated cases, so channel guides have something to stick to POG books installed on a clear hook and plastic sleeve for every set without shelf strips — tables, artisan wall, refrigerated and frozen bunkers No substitutions, ever. A facing with no product stays blank Fifteen minutes out of the case, not twenty. Bakery product is delicate and melts fast That last one is the biggest departure from the rest of this document. In grocery, an out-of-stock facing gets a dummy facing to hold the space. In bakery it stays empty. Don't carry the grocery habit across.

heading: Getting started
text: Check in at the front desk so the store knows you're on site and starting the bakery reset Find the Kompass cart in the back room. It should hold your materials, tools, and the bakery planogram Locate the Black ID tags. They ship with the shelf tags, but depending on the store they may be somewhere else. If you can't find them, ask the store's File Maintenance Coordinator or store management — they're usually with batches of price tags Take a before photo of the set or table you're about to start Tiered tables usually need more than one before photo — one of each side, front and back, to capture everything on it.

heading: Reading the bakery planogram
text: The front page tells you which set it covers — Breakfast, Ambient Cupcakes, Refrigerated Case — shows product images for each facing, and lists fixture dimensions so you can confirm you have the right set. The back of the first page is the Add/Delete page. It tells you what to remove and what to ask the bakery team for. Orientation: read the planogram standing with your back to the front of the store. Table 1 is the one closest to you. Table 5 is the furthest away. The remaining pages number every product by table and position. Column What it means Face How many facings the table needs of that product Face D A suggestion only. The division dictates stack height — follow division direction, not this number Face D is the one to watch. Everywhere else in this document the planogram is the authority; here one column isn't.

heading: Black ID tags
text: Every product on the bakery tables and the artisan bread wall gets a black ID tag . Event type What the store receives Kompass Update A tag for every facing — an item with 4 facings gets 4 tags NII or maintenance Tags only for the items that are changing

heading: The rules
text: Remove all old tags first , then wipe the table free of dust and debris Every product gets a fresh tag — even one that already has a tag and isn't moving Never stack a new tag on an old one. The old one comes off first, always

heading: Placement
text: Centered under the product and fully hidden , oriented the way the product faces. Horizontal product, horizontal tag and text. Vertical product, vertical tag and text.

heading: When black ID tags are missing
text: Make a temporary tag. Never skip a facing. With the handheld and tag printer: Put a blank black ID tag in the facing position Print an item label with the description and UPC Apply the white label on top of the blank black tag Without access to the handheld and printer: Put a blank black ID tag in the facing position Affix a Post-it with that item's UPC on top of it That lets the store print the white label on their Zebra and apply it over the black tag. Older paperwork calls that device a Telxon or Telson — same thing.

heading: Bakery tables
text: Remove all deleted items using the delete page. Once you've gathered them, find someone in the bakery department and let them tell you where to put them Remove all remaining product and all old black ID tags , then wipe the table clean Place the new black ID tags following the numbered guide on page 2 of the planogram Reading direction changes partway across. Left to right for Tables 1, 2, and the front half of Table 3. Right to left for the back half of Table 3 and Tables 4–5. Center each tag, oriented the way the product will face Every facing gets a fresh tag, whether or not the product moved Put product back. If there are holes for new product, ask the bakery department to help you find it. If a new product isn't in the store, leave the facing blank — no substitute product, no improvising. That's the store's call, not yours Swap the POG book on the side of the table Take your after photos — again, more than one for a tiered table Capture the reset in the Store Intelligence app for Kompass compliance

heading: The POG book
text: Remove and dispose of the previous book, slide the new POG into the plastic sleeve, put it back on the hook Check with your Deli/Bakery Merchandiser on whether they want POG books installed for additional sets Hook and sleeve should be available after the stand-up process, and the set team should have spares Missing hook or sleeve? Notify store management and the bakery team so they can pull a replacement from the school and hardware section No sleeve at all — hand the planogram directly to a bakery team member. Never leave it loose

heading: Refrigerated and frozen
text: Pull all the old strips from the current set Pull the deleted items using the add/delete page, and have a bakery team member direct you where they go. Refrigerated items go to refrigerated backstock , frozen to frozen backstock — so nothing gets put away wrong Remove everything and clean the shelves thoroughly. Check whether the black magnetic strips or channel guides need replacing — magnetic black tape is part of the supplies for refrigerated sets. If channels are missing and you don't have what you need to fix it, contact me Food safety: 15 minutes in bakery — not the 20 you get everywhere else. Refrigerated and frozen bakery product is never out of the case longer than fifteen minutes. Bakery items are delicate and they melt fast. Frosting slumps, cream and mousse soften, and glazes go tacky well before a case of frozen vegetables would even start to sweat. Damage here shows on the product, and a customer can see it. Stage your work so product goes back quickly. Pull what you can put back. Cut the new shelf strips along the dotted line to fit. Refrigerated shelves usually run 56 inches to 5 feet , and strips only come in 3-foot and 4-foot increments — expect multiple bays and spare strips Channel guides go in with the open edge facing down , so crumbs can't fill the channel. Guides first, then the strips into the guides. Replace the strips and hang all new tags provided Move product back to match the new strips , then fill holes with new product. Ask bakery where the new items are. Not in store? Facing stays blank After photos, then capture in Store Intelligence

heading: Bunkers and mobile cases — M1, Q2, SIM
text: Mirrors the table process, with one difference: the tags mount on magnetic tape. This covers the M1 bunker and the Q2 and SIM mobile cases. Same procedure for all three. Remove deleted items, and have bakery direct you where they go Remove all remaining product and all black ID tags, then wipe the bunker clean Use the guide on page 4 of the POG and follow the numbered products left to right. Magnetic tape should be on hand — cut it to the size of each black ID tag and stick the tag to the tape - Center each tag, oriented the way the product faces - Every facing gets a fresh tag - If the case won't take magnetic tape, use double-sided sticky tape instead. Not every bunker or mobile case is magnetic-compatible, and the tag still has to go on Put product back. Holes for new product — ask bakery. Not in store — leave the facing blank The 15-minute bakery rule applies here too. The bunker holds refrigerated and frozen product, and it's delicate for the same reasons. Work in stages so nothing sits out.

heading: Artisan bread wall
text: Remove all product and all black ID tags Pull the deleted items using the add/delete page, and have bakery direct you where they go Wipe the shelves down Add the black ID tags following the planogram Move product back to match, then fill holes with new product No shelf strips and no sale tags on the artisan wall — black ID tags only. Everything is priced as marked, and prices vary by size. After photos, then capture in Store Intelligence No substitutions. Facing stays blank if the product isn't in store.

heading: Racks and baskets
text: Covers the Colossal Cookie Rack , 3-tier baskets, and the other racks in the department. You'll get a planogram guide for any bakery change on any rack Find the right rack , pull all product, and remove all black ID tags from the back of the rack . Clean off dust and debris Place the new black ID tags along the back of the rack , following the planogram Two things are different here. Tags go on the back of the rack, not the front. And each UPC gets one tag — not one per facing, the way tables work. Add product to the rack per the planogram After photos, then capture in Store Intelligence

heading: Packaged bread destination
text: Remove all product, and remove the strips, tags, and channels Pull the deleted items using the add/delete page, and have bakery direct you where they go Wipe the shelves down Add the new shelf strips and channels per the planogram Put product back to match the new strips , then fill holes with new product. Not in store — facing stays blank The display has four sides. Bay 1 is Bakery Facing — the side facing the bakery tables. Bays 2 through 4 continue left to right: Front End , Outside, Back End. After photos, then capture in Store Intelligence

heading: The Kompass Bakery Completion Standard
text: The bakery team supports us — finding product, telling us where deletes go. Don't expect them to complete any part of the reset. The reset is ours, start to finish. Before you leave the store, all six of these are done: 1 The reset is 100% complete. Blank facings stay blank where product is unavailable — never substitutions 2 Fresh black ID tags on every facing. Missing tags follow the temporary tag process — never skip a facing 3 All materials handled. Unused labels and the old POG handed to a bakery team member — nothing left behind 4 The POG book is swapped on every set , and any missing hook or sleeve is replaced from the school and hardware section 5 After photos taken and uploaded to Store Intelligence — every side, every set 6 Walk the completed set before you leave — reps with their lead, leads with the store. Section 9.1

heading: If you can't finish
text: Contact me before you leave the store — not after. We'll make a plan together. We never hand unfinished work to the store. Read this before your next bakery visit. Questions on any of it — ask me before the reset, not after.

heading: Part II — Kompass Commodities
text: Part II — Kompass Commodities A commodity is a grouping of like items — pickles, laundry detergent, frozen pizza. Same thing this document calls a set , seen from the store's side rather than the shelf's. Every commodity has a number , and that number appears on the shelf strip and in the planogram code. Sections 7.1 and 7.7 cover where to find it. This is the Kompass list. These are the categories the program covers. A commodity that isn't here generally isn't part of this program — useful to know before you go hunting for a planogram that was never going to exist. Two ways to use this: the department view shows what's in scope for a department. The numeric index goes the other way — read a number off a strip, find out what it is. Recent change: Pet moved to Department 03 All Pet planogram names now read Department 03 instead of Department 01 , following a change to the family tree. Ten commodities are affected — wet and dry dog food, dog treats, wet and dry cat food, cat treats, cat litter, wild bird and animal feed, frozen and refrigerated pet food, and pet care supplies. What this means at the shelf: a pet planogram code now carries D03 where it used to carry D01 . Older paperwork, older planogram printouts, and anyone's memory will still say 01. The set hasn't moved and the work hasn't changed — only the department it files under. Marked ‡ in the list below. Rows marked † are commodities we still work that aren't on the current corporate list. Filter by number or name By department By number

heading: Part II — Conditioning and Stocking by Department
text: Part II — Conditioning and Stocking by Department Conditioning is bringing a shelf back to how it's meant to look — product pulled forward, faced, straightened, gaps closed. It's what makes a set look stocked when it's half sold. Two things to know before the department rules: You condition what you worked, and the scope follows the project. Project Condition Full reset The entire set you reset NII, partial, maintenance The area you worked , and no further This isn't about doing less. Work is time-allocated, and an NII may be allocated fifteen minutes. Conditioning a forty-foot aisle is not inside fifteen minutes, and pretending otherwise means either the job runs long or the actual work gets rushed to make room for it. It's the same discipline as Section 8.6 : you touch what you were sent to touch. Work outside your area isn't tracked, isn't signed off, and comes out of the next job. Every department does this differently, and the differences aren't arbitrary. Grocery is pulled forward. Frozen is stocked back to front. Dairy is built like a wall. Each one follows from how the product sells and how the case is built, so the rule that feels wrong in one department is the right rule in another.

heading: Grocery
text: Unstacked product — where the strip and planogram show no stacking: Pull three items forward for each facing Everything else stays pushed to the back of the shelf Stacked product — where the strip and planogram call for it: First layer: front to back Every layer above that: back to front That alternation is what stops the stack leaning forward. Build every layer front-to-back and the top of the stack walks toward the shelf edge. Caps go on top. A cap is a unit laid flat over standing product — the C in the C/H/W notation on the strip. See Section 7.7 . CSD 12-packs: handles face right. Every one, so the row reads as a block rather than a jumble. Chips and salty snacks are the exception to all of the above. They get pushed to the back for the vendor to fill. Don't pull them forward. This is DSD product and the vendor works it on their own schedule.

heading: Drug / GM
text: Most of this department is in pushers, and the pusher does the conditioning for you. Product not in a pusher gets pulled forward Never stock behind a pusher. The pusher is the back of the space — product behind it can't come forward and won't be found Only lay product on top of pusher product if the planogram says to. Otherwise the paddle jams Every peg hook needs an inventory control clip , with product merchandised to the front of the peg. The ICC is what holds it there — a peg without one drifts back within a day and reads as empty from down the aisle See Part II, Special Fixtures for the pusher and peg hardware itself.

heading: Dairy
text: Build it like a wall. Left to right, and upward where the product stacks. Fill the front of the shelf completely before you start filling toward the back All empty space ends up at the back of the shelf , never at the front That's the opposite of the grocery habit of pulling forward, and it's deliberate: dairy sells fast and gets refilled constantly, so the case is worked from the front and the gap belongs where the customer doesn't see it. Clean before you reload. Back walls of the cases, the wire grates, the area under the grates — the well — and the shelves. The well is the part everyone skips and it's the part that gets checked. Milk racks carry two sets of strips: one customer-facing, one inside the cooler. Set one and you've done half the job. Anyone loading from the back of the rack is reading the inside strip.

heading: Frozen
text: Everything in frozen is stocked back to front. The reverse of grocery. On the bottom shelf — the well — lay product down wherever possible. When a shelf holds more than one layer: The lays go down first , flat on the shelf The standing product goes on top of the lays Not the other way round. Product laid across the top of standing items is unstable, hides what's underneath, and falls out when a customer takes one Every product gets as many lays as will fit, plus one standing item. The standing item is the one the customer reads. Top shelf: two standing items pulled forward. Pizza is the exception — all pizzas on the bottom shelf stand. They're wide and flat and a stack of laid pizzas can't be got at. Items marked SRP on the strip stay in their display boxes. Don't unpack them. Twenty minutes out of the case, maximum. Then it goes into the walk-in freezer. Watch which one you put it in — frozen product in a cooler is a write-off, and so is the reverse.

heading: Front end
text: Checklanes, self-checkouts, and tobacco cases work differently enough to have their own section. See Part II, Front End .

heading: Part II — Front End
text: Part II — Front End The front end is the checklanes, the self-checkouts, and the service desk. It's the last thing a customer passes and the busiest floor space in the building, and it's set differently enough from an aisle to need its own rules. Three things make it different: Everything is described from the customer's point of view, not yours The fixtures are small, and the hardware is specific to them — 6-inch pegs, tag holders, tiny racks bolted to machines You are working in the one part of the store that never really closes

heading: Customer left, customer right
text: Stand in the lane, facing the front of the store — the way a customer moves through it. Now left is customer left and right is customer right. Every checklane and self-checkout merchandiser is identified this way, on the planogram and in conversation. It does not change based on which way you happen to be standing while you work. Get this backwards and you'll build a mirror image of the planogram, correctly, and have to strip it. Orient yourself before you start, not after.

heading: Tails
text: The tail is the part of a manned checklane where product is merchandised — the merchandiser unit running alongside the belt. You'll see it written as a size on the planogram: Size MED Medium tail LG Large tail XL Extra large So a planogram headed MED TAIL CHECKLANE is telling you which physical unit it's built for. Check that against the lane in front of you before you set anything — lanes in the same store aren't all the same size.

heading: Match the planogram to the setup
text: Checklanes aren't uniform. Before you start, confirm the planogram matches what's actually in the lane: Cooler orientation — rear-facing or side-facing Snack configuration KPF — Kroger Personal Finance, the gift card and telecom fixtures A planogram built for a side-facing cooler won't set onto a rear-facing one, and finding that out at position 1 is much cheaper than finding out at position 20.

heading: Peg hardware
text: Checklanes use 6-inch peg hooks. Not the 11-inch pegs used on aisle peg sets Every hook needs a clear plastic tag holder Every hook needs an inventory control clip , with the product pulled forward and held at the front of the hook by the ICC That combination — 6-inch hook, tag holder, ICC — is the standard checklane peg. A hook missing any of the three isn't finished.

heading: Self-checkouts
text: SCOs are set the same way as manned lanes and laid out differently in every store.

heading: The two layouts
text: Layout 6-pack A group of six machines — three on customer left, three on customer right Bullpen / corral A larger group arranged around the perimeter of an area, with one entrance and one exit Which one a store has changes how you walk the set and how many merchandisers you're working with. Look at the layout before you start rather than assuming it matches the last store.

heading: The fixtures
text: Candy and gift card racks sit around each machine , and they're identified by the model of the machine — Toshiba SCO -6, Toshiba SCO-7, and so on. The model determines which racks fit. If a rack won't mount, check the machine model against the planogram before you force anything. SCO coolers carry merchandising racks too. They're either single or double rear-facing coolers, and the planogram will specify which.

heading: Tobacco cases
text: Tobacco is a locked, regulated set, and it has two rules that don't apply anywhere else in the store.

heading: Where the cases are
text: Case Where Short cases Usually by the self-checkouts or the customer service desk Tall cases Along the front wall, occasionally behind the customer service desk Fuel center cases The fuel center has its own

heading: The state rule
text: Different states have different tobacco planograms. Confirm the planogram you're holding is for the correct state before you touch the case. This is the one place in the building where setting the wrong plan isn't just wrong, it's a regulatory problem. Check it every time, even in a store you've set before.

heading: Setting the case
text: Verify shelf heights first , same as any reset Work from the bottom of the case to the top Cigarettes go in 4- or 5- pusher sections that lock into the case shelves Smokeless tobacco uses its own pushers — rounded front, and they lock into the shelf the same way Anything not in a pusher is stocked front to back

heading: Digital shelf labels at the front end
text: Checklanes are explicitly in the rollout. They're one of the four places DSL currently goes, and the parts are specific to them — the checkout hardware family in the parts reference, including the wire fence locking holder and the suspension hook with button clips. Everything else at the front end is currently out. Tobacco, gift cards, clip strips, seasonal , American Greetings, and the service departments all sit outside the rollout for now. So do freestanding displays and the fuel center. Section 8 , Step 8 has the install and association procedure. The do-not-install list is current, not permanent, so check with your lead if you're unsure.
