heading: Part II — Special Fixtures
text: Part II — Special Fixtures A shelf is a shelf. Everything else on the front edge, the back wall, or hanging off the gondola is a fixture with a job — holding product forward as stock runs down, keeping items that won't stack from falling over, making things reachable, or turning a flat gondola into something that displays a spatula. This section is for looking things up. You don't need to read it front to back. When you get to a set and find hardware you don't recognize, find it here. One thing to get straight before anything else: " rail " means two different parts. A pusher rail is the plastic track along the shelf front that pushers and end pieces lock into. An ESL rail is the clip-in channel that holds a digital shelf label. They sit in the same place and do unrelated jobs. Section 8 , Step 4 covers the ESL rail.

heading: Pushers
text: Empty pusher tracks installed side by side on a shelf before product is loaded. Clear pusher plates on black track rails — the front fence holds product at the shelf edge. A standalone clear divider used to separate product lanes on a shelf. Single black pusher track with spring-loaded front mechanism and clear product stop. Clear pusher channel — the black housing at the front contains the spring that pushes product forward. Disassembled pusher hardware — tray base and divider plate before installation. Lunch meat cooler with pusher-equipped shelves keeping product faced to the front. Complete pusher lane unit — black base tray, upright paddle, and clear front fence. Produce section showing refrigerated pusher shelves alongside open produce displays. Cooler base with fan and refrigerant lines exposed — shelf tilted for maintenance access. A pusher is a spring-loaded fixture that keeps product pushed to the front of the shelf as stock sells down. It's the reason a DGM shelf still looks full with four items left on it.

heading: The three components
text: Part What it is Rail The plastic track fitted along the front of the shelf. Everything else locks into it Pusher / divider The spring-loaded paddle on a track. Its length matches or is shorter than the shelf depth. The paddle rotates and sets to different positions to take different product widths and heights. Comes in single and double End pieces Left and right side pieces. Ends go only at the beginning and end of the set — not between bays if the set continues across several That last rule catches people. If a category runs across three bays, you get one left end at the very start and one right end at the very finish. Putting ends at every bay seam breaks the run into three sets that look like they were done by three different people.

heading: Setting a pusher shelf
text: Lay out the pusher positions before you fill anything. Space them evenly across the shelf first, then load. Filling as you go leaves you with the last pusher crammed against the end piece Don't stock product behind a pusher. The pusher is the back of the space. Product behind it can't move forward and won't be found Product not in a pusher gets pulled forward — that's the general DGM rule Only lay product on top of pusher product if the planogram says so. Otherwise the paddle jams

heading: Coffee pushers
text: Different shape, same three components, installed the same way. Don't be thrown by the profile .

heading: Grid pushers — smoked meat, frozen meat and seafood, bagged salad
text: These work differently and the planogram will mislead you if you don't know it. A metal grid mounts to the back wall of the freezer or refrigerated case Two-part pushers hang on that grid The planogram may show these sections as ordinary shelves. They aren't. Each facing sits in its own separate pusher Lay out the pusher spacing across the grid before filling, same as any pusher shelf Air baffles. If a smoked meat or produce set has no doors , plastic air baffles go between each row of pushers. These are not optional trim — they're what makes the cold air circulate through the case. Leave them out and the product at the front of the case sits warmer than it should. In Produce: pre-packaged and bagged salad is always in pushers. Carrots and mushrooms are sometimes in pushers — it varies store to store, so look before you assume.

heading: DSL note
text: Bagged salad pushers have their own digital label holder — the Salad Pusher System Adapter ESL Holder . If you're in a DSL store setting salad, that's the part you're looking for. The parts reference has the number.

heading: Sets that use pushers
text: Standard across the division, though individual stores vary. Health and OTC : antacids · cold and cough · sinus and allergy · analgesics (internal pain) · external pain · foot care · sports · smoke · family planning · vitamins · natural vitamins · eye and ear care · first aid · pediatrics Personal care: his shave · her shave · his deodorant · her deodorant · facial · lotion · sun care (not always) · cotton · hair color · denture · toothpaste Baby: baby wipes (top two shelves) · diapers (top two shelves) · baby HBC Special pushers: coffee · bagged salad Perishable, on grids: smoked meat · pre-packaged lunch meat · frozen seafood · frozen meat

heading: Pegboards and bump-outs
text: Single bracket mounted to a pegboard — the oval slot hooks over a pegboard hole. Bracket installation detail — one screw anchors the top slot to the pegboard. Pegboard with nine brackets in a grid pattern — used to lay out bumpout mounting positions. Shelf bracket engaged in the upright slot — the stamped number 20 marks the bracket depth.

heading: Peg hooks
text: 11-inch peg hooks are standard on peg sets His Shave and Her Shave use 8-inch pegs — unless the Relay Manager instructs otherwise Checklanes use 6-inch pegs. See Part II, Front End Every peg hook needs an inventory control clip (ICC) with the product merchandised to the front of the peg. The ICC is what holds it there. A peg without one drifts back within a day and reads as empty from down the aisle Hook types you'll meet: fast-back hooks (two-prong, sometimes two-part for easy removal), J hooks (mounted on a shelf rather than a board, usually impulse product), and sky hook pegs .

heading: Frogs
text: The frog is the plastic clip that seats into the pegboard and holds the peg hook. Set one on a table and you'll see where the name comes from — the two legs and the body read as a frog sitting there. A frog occupies two holes, and that raises an obvious question: which hole is the position? The left leg goes into the hole specified. That's the whole convention, and it's worth committing to memory, because a frog seated one hole off puts the product one inch off — and every peg you hang after it inherits the error. Combined with the one-inch rule: the specified hole takes the left leg, and the frog spans that hole and the one immediately to its right.

heading: The one-inch rule
text: Pegboard holes are exactly one inch apart, center to center — both across and down. Learn this one. It converts every peg instruction in this document from counting to measuring, and a tape measure finds a position faster and more reliably than your eyes count holes. Three holes over is three inches over A 3 × 3 hardware grid is a three-inch grid A peg position from the schematic can be measured to instead of counted to

heading: Bump-outs — what they are
text: Reference, not a task. You won't build one of these. Construction does. But you will move them, audit them, and work around them, so you need to recognize what you're looking at and be able to tell whether one is right. A bump-out is a pegboard extended away from the gondola , so pegged product sits further forward and is easier for a customer to reach. All peg sets get bumped out. Trial size isn't on pegs — it has its own bins — and those get bumped out too. Three components: bars, brackets, and the pegboard itself. Component What it does Pegboard The perforated board, cut to size for the bay Brackets Nine of them, mounted to the back of the board on a 3 × 3 grid . The corner brackets sit three holes in from each edge — three inches, by the one-inch rule Extender bars Three bars hung on the gondola the same way a shelf hangs. The board hangs on these What "right" looks like: the board sits square and doesn't rock, and all nine brackets are seated on the bars. A board that moves when you push it has a bracket that isn't seated, and that's worth reporting rather than living with — a loaded pegboard that comes off the bars takes the product with it.

heading: Magna-Bars
text: This one you do work on. Moving, resetting, and hanging Magna-Bars is regular work, so know the system rather than just recognizing it. Not the same as a bump-out, though they're close cousins. A bump-out hangs a pegboard on bars. A Magna-Bar is the bar, with hooks going straight into it and no board at all. Similar hardware family, different system — don't order one expecting the other. A Magna-Bar is a peg merchandising system that mounts to the gondola uprights directly. Peg hooks hang off the bar itself, so there's no pegboard involved — it's an alternative to a peg wall, not a component of one. Bars come in horizontal and vertical, and the system takes ID channels that carry the shelf strip. Components , per the manufacturer's kit of four bars: Part Count per 4 bars Bars 4 Brackets 8 — one at each end of each bar Uprights 8 Flat plates 8 Screws 16

heading: FRONT AND UP
text: The bar is stamped FRONT AND UP. That stamp is not a label — it's the mechanism. The end of the peg hook that goes into the bar is D-shaped , and so are the slots along the bar. The flat of the D has to meet the flat of the slot. Get that right and the hook drops in and locks . Get it wrong and the shapes don't marry up — the hook either won't go in, or it sits in the slot without ever locking, which is worse, because it looks fine until the product on it takes it off the wall. So: Mount the bar with FRONT AND UP reading correctly, and the hooks lock. Mount it inverted or reversed, and they don't. When you pull a bar to move it, check the stamp on the way back in. Don't trust the orientation you found it in — if it was wrong before, putting it back the same way keeps it wrong, and now it's wrong on your set. If a hook won't seat, or seats but slides back out, check the bar's orientation before you do anything else. That's the cause far more often than a damaged hook. Load limit: 150 lbs per bar. A sagging bar is a report, not something to shim. What "right" looks like: FRONT AND UP reading correctly, brackets seated in the upright slots at both ends, all screws tight, bar level, and hooks that lock in rather than rest in.

heading: Dividers and clearview
text: Clearview divider strip — transparent rail with repeating slot openings. Another clearview divider profile — serrated top edge and segmented sections. Dried beans faced in clear dividers — each stack held in its own lane. Rice and grains set on multiple shelves — products stacked deep behind the front facing. Office and school supplies on pegboard and shelf — notebooks and stationery in organized rows. Black U-channel divider — matte outer surface with felt-like inner lining. Black divider channel with clear front stop — shown before installation on the shelf. Empty glide shelf in a cooler — white plastic tracks and dividers with no product loaded. Both keep product that doesn't stack well from sliding, leaning, or migrating into the next facing. Both attach to the shelf with plastic "Christmas tree" clips. Fixture What it does Divider A plastic insert that separates facings — a wall between one product and the next Clearview A clear plastic strip mounted along the shelf front that stops items sliding off Fencing is the same idea under an older name from the acquired companies — an acrylic or metal rail along the shelf front.

heading: Sets that use them
text: Whether a set gets dividers, clearview, or both is the Relay Manager's call on that project. Set Fixture Tortillas Dividers, clearview, or both Marshmallows Dividers, clearview, or both Beans and rice (bag section) Dividers, clearview, or both Rice cakes Dividers between SKUs, not between facings Pasta (bag sections) Dividers, clearview, or both School and office Dividers, clearview, or both Natural chips ( top stock shelf) Clearview only Chips (bases) Clearview only — 1-inch

heading: Slides
text: Clearview divider strip — transparent rail with repeating slot openings. Another clearview divider profile — serrated top edge and segmented sections. Dried beans faced in clear dividers — each stack held in its own lane. Rice and grains set on multiple shelves — products stacked deep behind the front facing. Office and school supplies on pegboard and shelf — notebooks and stationery in organized rows. Black U-channel divider — matte outer surface with felt-like inner lining. Black divider channel with clear front stop — shown before installation on the shelf. Empty glide shelf in a cooler — white plastic tracks and dividers with no product loaded. A slide does what a divider does, except the product sits inside it. That makes stocking and conditioning faster — you pull the whole row forward instead of straightening each item. Slide Where Spice slide Numbered by size. Spices, canned cat food, and dry desserts (gelatin and pudding). Check the number — they aren't interchangeable Yogurt slide Has a built-in handle to pull the row forward Creamer slide Refrigerated coffee creamer in dairy, mounted on the milk racks

heading: In-line single-serve cases
text: Single-serve energy drinks and sodas faced on cooler shelves with lane dividers. Single-serve cans on slanted cooler tracks — product loaded on its side in gravity-feed lanes. Single-serve beverage cases use roller shelves — the shelf floor is a set of rollers, so when a customer takes a can the row behind it flows forward on its own. Two things have to be right or it doesn't work: Every facing or row needs a divider. Without one, rows merge and the flow jams Clearview must be snapped securely into the front of each roller shelf. It's the only thing stopping the front can rolling onto the floor

heading: Kitchen Place and the in-line kitchen grid
text: Kitchen place grid fixtures — small tools on pegboard panels beside boxed cookware on gondola shelves. Inline kitchen grid section — pegboard tool walls behind freestanding dinnerware display tables. Household kitchen accessories don't sit on ordinary shelves. They're merchandised on grids , and which style you find depends on the store format. Format Where Kitchen Place Marketplace, Expanded, and Upscale stores. Free-standing gridwall with display tables in front In-line kitchen grid Food and Value stores. Grid panels set into the run itself Both hang product from the grid rather than standing it on a shelf, so peg and hook rules apply rather than facing and stack rules. One storage exception worth knowing: there is no top stock in Kitchen Place stores. See Part II, Storage .

heading: Part II — Storage
text: Part II — Storage Excess product is anything that won't fit on the shelf. Before you decide where it goes, understand why there's excess at all. Inventory and allocations are calculated from the shelf's depth capacity — how much the set is designed to hold. When a shelf is stocked exactly as the planogram says, the ordering system is working from a true number. When it isn't, the store orders against a shelf that doesn't exist. So the first rule of storage is a setting rule: stock the shelf exactly as the planogram indicates, then deal with what's left over. Don't cram an extra layer on to avoid a trip to the back. Excess goes to one of three places: top stock , a U-boat , or backstock storage.

heading: Top stock
text: The shelf above the set. Some older paperwork calls it a riser . Why it exists: product on top stock is above the set it belongs to, in the aisle, where anyone can reach it. That keeps the back room emptier and makes replenishment something a store associate does in thirty seconds instead of a trip to the back and a hunt through a pallet.

heading: Setting top stock
text: Pull items forward , labels facing forward Leave the left-hand item turned so its UPC faces out. Someone scanning to replenish shouldn't have to lift and rotate a case to find the barcode No more than three high Product must sit above the set it belongs to. Don't top stock pasta above mustard — top stock is a location system as well as a storage one, and product above the wrong set is lost Tray packs and SRP product can go on the top shelf directly , labels forward, left item's UPC turned out Unopened cases don't get top stocked — tray packs and SRP excepted Large or heavy items don't go up top at all. Charcoal, dog food, bulk liquids. Those go on a Fast or Active backstock cart instead. A case you have to lift over your head is a case you shouldn't be lifting over your head Organize the top shelf as you go. It's maintained daily, not rebuilt weekly

heading: Where top stock is not allowed
text: Exception Kitchen Place stores No top stock at all. See Part II, Special Fixtures Infant formula Never top stocked From a display No more than two cases on the top shelf above the home location

heading: U-boats
text: A U-boat is the green six-wheeled cart — narrow, and U-shaped in profile , which is where the name comes from. Fred Meyer uses them for vendor stock and backstock. Get them from the receiver in the back room Walked, never ridden or coasted. Six wheels and a long narrow frame means it goes where it's pointed and keeps going Don't leave a loaded U-boat in an aisle. Same rule as carts — if nobody's actively working off it, it's out of the aisle Return them to the receiver at the end of the shift

heading: Backstock storage
text: What doesn't go up top and isn't on a cart goes into containers.

heading: What to put it in
text: Banana boxes, first and almost always. They're the container of choice for this work and they're what you'll use nearly every shift. Sturdy, stackable, a sensible size for a person to carry loaded, and with a lid that lets them stack without crushing what's underneath. Get them from produce or from the receiver. Blue Peyton totes second , when banana boxes aren't available. Beyond those two, ask your lead. Other containers exist in the store — bread trays, meat crates, egg crates, produce crates, milk crates — and older reference material lists them as fallbacks, but they aren't what this division uses and you shouldn't reach for one on your own initiative.

heading: Stacking
text: Don't stack more than 6 high , and use judgment below that — a stack you can't see over, or can't get a hand under to move, is too tall regardless of the count.

heading: Two rules that aren't about tidiness
text: Never mix food and chemicals on the same pallet. That's a food safety issue, and it's the kind of thing that gets noticed in an audit long after everyone's forgotten who stacked it Never store liquids on their sides. Under the pressure of a stack, they leak — and a leak inside a stack isn't found until it's soaked through several layers

heading: Handing it off
text: A boxed-up box isn't finished. It has to end up somewhere someone will act on. Ask the receiver first. If they can take it now, or soon, leave it with them. That's the clean outcome — it's their process from that point and it doesn't sit anywhere. If they won't have time soon, palletize it. A stack of boxes on the floor of the back room is in someone's way and will be moved by someone who doesn't know what's in it. On a pallet it's stable, it's movable, and it stays together. Either way, every box is clearly labeled. This is the part that gets skipped at the end of a shift and it's the part that matters most. An unlabeled box is a guess — for the receiver, for the next team in, for whoever eventually opens it. A pallet of unlabeled boxes is a pallet nobody unpacks, and it sits in the back room until someone gives up and works through it one box at a time. Label it with the category: Backstock · Discontinued · Not In Set · Damaged · Expired One of those five, on every box. That's what the receiver sorts by, and it's the difference between a box that gets processed and a box that gets opened, puzzled over, and set down again. Label as you fill, not at the end. You know what's in the box while you're putting it in there.

heading: Sorting what comes off the shelf
text: At the start of the shift your lead designates and signs an area for each of these. Ask where they are before you need them. The five box labels are the five categories. Sort into them as you pull, and the labeling takes care of itself. Label What goes in it Backstock Product that won't fit on the shelf. Top stock or a U-boat first; what's left gets boxed Discontinued DIs per the Kompass Notes , carrying closeout tags Not In Set Product that isn't on this planogram. Marked down for clearance or returned to the DSD vendor Damaged Torn boxes, cut bags, smashed cans, leaking cartons. Not sellable Expired Past its sell-by or expiration date Trash — cardboard, plastic, waste — isn't boxed or labeled. It's disposed of properly as you go. Everything from one set stays together. If the pickle set comes off, all of it goes in the same place — carts, totes, milk crates, bread trays, whatever you're using — until it goes back to its permanent home. Splitting a pulled set across three locations turns a twenty-minute job into an hour. Take it to its area within a reasonable time. Not at the end of the shift. Carts full of product are not left in aisles, and a cart that isn't being actively worked comes out of the aisle — see Section 8.1 for the one-cart-per-person rule. Refrigerated and frozen product gets 20 minutes out of the case , then it goes into the walk-in cooler or freezer. Check which one you're putting it in — refrigerated product in a freezer is a write-off, and so is the reverse. Bakery runs tighter — 15 minutes. Frosting, cream, and glazes go before anything else does. See Part II, Bakery .

heading: Adjacency
text: How sets sit next to each other along an aisle. The store-layout view of the same idea as **aisle sequence**.

heading: Aisle marker
text: The sign hanging over each aisle listing the commodities found in it. Two styles, both filled with verbiage inserts selected by which commodities have the most footage.

heading: Aisle navigation
text: Collectively, the aisle markers and outriggers that get a customer from the main aisle to a specific set.

heading: Associate (a tag)
text: Pairing a DSL tag to its shelf position: open the DSL app, scan the tag, scan the shelf strip, confirm *Matched Successfully*, move on. Don't stand there watching it.

heading: Back room
text: The stockroom and receiving area. Where the receiver works and where new-item stock comes from.

heading: Back tag
text: A printed card hung from a peg hook when the product is out of stock. Carries the facings, SKU, and description so the peg keeps its place.

heading: Backstock
text: Product that won't fit on the shelf. It goes to top stock, onto a **U-boat**, or into **banana boxes** — never left sitting in the aisle. See Part II, Storage.

heading: Baler
text: The cardboard compactor in the back room. You must be 18 or older and be shown that specific machine before operating it.

heading: Banana box
text: The container we use for backstock, first choice and near enough the only one. Sturdy, stackable, lidded, and sized so a loaded one is still liftable. From produce or the receiver.

heading: Base shelf
text: The bottom shelf of a bay. Sits on the shoe and has no prongs, which is what makes it different from an upper.

heading: Bay
text: Each 4-foot segment of a gondola. Occasionally 3 feet depending on the store. Bays are numbered left to right within a commodity.

heading: Blitz
text: A rapid rollout of a product or planogram across a whole area at once, usually timed to an ad date.

heading: Bump-out
text: A section of pegboard extended away from the gondola so pegged product is easier to reach. Three components: bars, brackets, pegboard. Also called an extended pegboard.

heading: CAO
text: A Fred Meyer system the store uses to sign work out. Retail Odyssey associates have no access and are not permitted to sign out work in them.

heading: Cap shelf
text: The top shelf on an endcap, in the promo aisle, or in the grocery lobby. Used for signage and seasonal décor only, not product.

heading: Caps / lays
text: Product placed flat, either underneath upright product in frozen or stacked on top of faced product elsewhere.

heading: CCCR
text: Customer Choice Checklane Reinvention. The checklane plan that weights product selection toward natural candy and snacks.

heading: Center store
text: The non-perishable departments: grocery, frozen, dairy, drug/GM, beer and wine. As opposed to the perishable perimeter.

heading: Channel
text: The indented front edge of a shelf, where the data skin mounts. See **data skin**.

heading: Channel strip
text: Another name for a data skin, from the channel it sits in. See **data skin**.

heading: Chest
text: A bunker or open freezer well. Counted differently from a shelf — see Section 7.10.

heading: Clearview
text: Clear plastic mounted to a shelf to stop items sliding off. Attaches with plastic "Christmas tree" clips.

heading: Clip strip
text: A thin plastic or metal strip with hooks down one side, hung to merchandise product outside its normal set.

heading: Cross-merchandising
text: The same product merchandised in more than one place in the store — batteries in electronics and at the checklane.

heading: Cut-in
text: Adding a new item into an existing planogram without rebuilding the set. What a partial project usually involves in a category without strips.

heading: Damaged product
text: Items whose packaging or contents are compromised: torn boxes, cut bags, smashed cans, leaking cartons. Not sellable. Comes off the set into a labeled box and goes to the receiver.

heading: Data skin
text: The clear plastic channel guide that snaps onto the front edge of a shelf and holds the strip. **This is the term we use.** You will also hear *channel*, *data channel*, and *channel strip* — all the same part. Correcting data skins is part of NII and DI work.

heading: DC (Display Compliance)
text: **A different job, not yours.** A separate team audits secondary locations of product against the marketing plan, store by store, on a weekly cycle. It's Retail Odyssey work but it isn't Kompass work — nothing in a DC scan touches your reset, and nothing in your reset feeds a DC scan.

heading: DGM
text: Drug / General Merchandise. Covers HBC, OTC, and general merchandise.

heading: DI
text: Discontinued item. Flagged in the Kompass Notes and marked on the shelf with a closeout tag. Comes off the set and goes to the store associate or into a labeled box.

heading: Disassociate
text: Clearing a DSL tag at the end of a set so it stops displaying a price. Open the app, select Disassociate, scan, confirm, and the tag goes back on the Kompass cart. **Every leftover tag gets cleared** — an active tag on an empty space is advertising a price for nothing.

heading: Distance from base shelf
text: Printed in red in small type on the shelf strip: how far that shelf sits above the base shelf. An independent check on shelf heights, taken from a fixed datum rather than measured up the bay. See Section 7.3.

heading: Distressed goods
text: See **damaged product**. The term the acquired companies use.

heading: Divider
text: Plastic insert mounted to a shelf to separate facings and keep items that don't stack well organized.

heading: DSD
text: Direct Store Delivery. Product the vendor orders, delivers, and stocks themselves — Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Frito-Lay. Not ordered or stocked by Kroger, and generally not yours to work.

heading: DSL / ESL
text: **Two names for one thing, and you'll see both in the same shift.**

heading: DSL app
text: The app on the Zebra used to associate and disassociate tags.

heading: Dummy facing
text: When the product isn't in stock, a same-size item turned **backwards** on the shelf to hold the space open. The hole stays the right width, and whoever fills it later doesn't have to re-measure. Backwards is the point — nobody buys it by mistake.

heading: Effective date
text: The date a planogram goes live in the store. Not the date it was created and not necessarily the date you work it.

heading: Endcap
text: A 3- or 4-foot section at the end of a gondola, used for seasonal, temporary, or promotional product.

heading: Facing
text: The number of one product placed side by side across the front of a shelf. Shown as **Fac** on the planogram position table and on the strip. Facings are horizontal only — depth is separate.

heading: Fast-back hook
text: A two-prong peg hook. Some are two-part for easy removal.

heading: Fencing
text: Acrylic or metal rail on the shelf front that keeps product from sliding off. Same job as clearview.

heading: Field App
text: Where your schedule, store assignment, lead's name, and special instructions live. prod.sasretail.com/en/field.

heading: Fixture
text: Any furnishing that holds merchandise: gondolas, pegboards, pushers, cases.

heading: Fresh / perishables
text: Meat, seafood, deli, bakery, produce. Found around the perimeter of the store.

heading: Frog
text: The plastic clip that seats into a pegboard and holds the peg hook. Named for its shape — the two legs and body look like a frog sitting on a table. It occupies **two holes**, and **the left leg goes into the hole specified.** See Part II, Special Fixtures.

heading: Front end
text: The manned checklanes, self-checkouts, and service desk.

heading: Front Runner
text: **This means two different things, and context tells you which.**

heading: Full reset
text: A complete rebuild of a category to a new planogram. See Section 8.

heading: Gondola
text: The shelving unit that holds the shelves — the main structure of an aisle, secured to the floor. Also called a **run**.

heading: Grocery receiving door
text: The loading dock at the back of the store where trucks unload. Usually how you get in — through the **man door** beside the dock, not the dock itself. Your lead will confirm.

heading: HBC
text: Health and Beauty Care. Non-medicinal personal care: body wash, soap, shampoo, conditioner, toothpaste, mouthwash.

heading: ICC (Inventory Control Clip)
text: Plastic device placed on a peg hook behind the product, limiting how many items fit on the peg and holding the product forward.

heading: J hook
text: A J-shaped hook mounted on a shelf, used for impulse product.

heading: J-2 skin
text: A clip-on data skin, one of the holders you'll meet on a DSL set.

heading: Key Retailing
text: Kroger's operating standards, including stock rotation.

heading: Kompass
text: Kroger Optimization Management Plan Aligning Store Sales. The program that keeps shelf sets current and aligned to plan. It's the job.

heading: Kompass cart
text: The store's staging cart holding new items, Notes, planograms, strips, and tags for the visit.

heading: Kompass Champion
text: The store's designated contact for the visit, typically the Operations Assistant Store Manager. Rarely staffed in practice; the Food Manager often stands in.

heading: Kompass Completion
text: The Fred Meyer system where the store signs work out. Store access only.

heading: Kompass Notes
text: The weekly instructions for what's changing at this store, including which items are discontinued.

heading: Kost Klip
text: The manufacturer of the ESL rails and holders. Their part numbers are what you order by.

heading: KPF
text: Kroger Personal Finance. Gift cards and telecom.

heading: LAMCOE
text: Layout & Mapping Center of Excellence. The team that maps planograms onto each store's floorplan, deciding which plan lands on which fixture.

heading: Lead in
text: The first product a customer sees coming from the main aisle. Planograms carry lead-in indicators showing which end of the set faces the main aisle.

heading: Magna-Bar
text: A peg merchandising system that mounts straight to the gondola uprights, with hooks hanging off the bar instead of a pegboard. **The bar is stamped FRONT AND UP, and that stamp is the mechanism, not a label** — the hook's shank and the bar's slots are both D-shaped, and the flats only meet when the bar is the right way up. Wrong way up, the hook rests in the slot without locking. Rated to 150 lbs. See Part II, Special Fixtures.

heading: Maintenance
text: A partial project correcting or updating part of a set.

heading: Man door
text: The normal person-sized door beside a loading dock. Drivers use it, and so do we. See **grocery receiving door**.

heading: Mapping
text: The planograms assigned to a particular store.

heading: NII
text: New Item Introduction. A partial project adding new products to an existing set.

heading: Not-in-set / not-on-POG / disco
text: Items no longer carried at that store. Either marked down for clearance or returned to the DSD vendor. Comes off the set.

heading: OOS
text: Out of stock. Item not available for sale.

heading: OTC
text: Over-the-Counter. Medicinal items: pain relief, first aid, vitamins and supplements.

heading: Out of date
text: Product past its sell-by or expiration date. Comes off the set.

heading: Outrigger
text: In-aisle signage mounted to the gondola identifying a specific set. Four styles depending on department and fixture type.

heading: Overstock
text: Product left over once the shelf is set to plan. Goes to the designated associate or into labeled overstock boxes.

heading: Part code
text: The short label on a shelf part, like H-1, J-3, or O-2. Use it to call a part out loud; use the **Part ID** to actually get one.

heading: Part ID
text: The six-digit number you order or request a shelf part by. Always order by Part ID, never by code — one part can carry two different codes.

heading: PCOE
text: Planogram Center of Excellence. The central team that builds the planograms. One plan, a whole division.

heading: Peg / peg hook
text: Metal or plastic hook fitted into a pegboard or grid to hang product.

heading: Pegboard
text: Perforated board used to hang peg hooks. **The holes are exactly one inch apart, center to center, both across and down.** That turns counting into measuring: a peg three holes over is three inches over, and a tape measure will find it faster than your eyes will.

heading: PIC
text: Person in Charge. The store associate running the building at that moment. Overnight, that is who your lead goes to when a manager isn't on site.

heading: POD
text: Storage trailers holding construction materials and remodel equipment. Remodel work, not weekly Kompass.

heading: POG (planogram)
text: The schematic showing exactly what product goes where, in what quantity. Also called a schematic. The authority for every set you build.

heading: Preferred product
text: Shelves between hip and eye level. The most valuable space on the gondola, which is why the plan puts specific items there.

heading: Price changer
text: The store associate who produces and corrects price tags. **This is the term we use.** The same person is also called the scan coordinator or pricing coordinator — one role, three names. A position you couldn't tag goes to your lead, and your lead takes it to them.

heading: Private label
text: A store's own brand. At Fred Meyer, **Our Brand**.

heading: Profile
text: Two senses, both about height: the overall height of a gondola, and the distance from one shelf to the next. *"Set it to the right profile"* means get the shelf heights right.

heading: Promo aisle
text: Also called the seasonal aisle. Product rotates by season or holiday.

heading: Pusher
text: Spring-loaded fixture keeping product pushed to the front of the shelf. Three components: rail, pusher/divider, end pieces.

heading: Rail
text: **Two different parts share this word.** A **pusher rail** is the plastic track on the shelf front that pushers and end pieces lock into. An **ESL rail** is the clip-in or clip-over channel that holds a digital shelf label. They sit in the same place on the shelf and do completely different jobs.

heading: Relay Manager
text: Fred Meyer's title for the person leading a remodel or relay overnight. Same role Kroger elsewhere calls a Remodel Team Leader. Not part of your escalation path — day-of issues go to your Team Lead, then to me.

heading: Reline
text: An overhaul of a shelf to rearrange product or bring it back to planogram.

heading: Reset
text: A major change to an existing planogram — a section, a department, or a whole store.

heading: Retail Logic
text: The technical name of the app you clock in and out on. Also called the **SAS Retail App**, and in conversation just the Field App. Same tool, three names.

heading: Riser
text: Shelving above the shoppable part of a gondola. Another name for the **top stock** shelf. Third name for the same shelf, so it's here to be looked up, not taught.

heading: ROM
text: Remodel Operations Manager. Kroger's person in charge of a remodel project. Not part of your escalation path.

heading: Rotate stock
text: Older product to the front, newer product to the back of each facing. Not optional, and invisible to anyone walking the finished set.

heading: RTL
text: Remodel Team Leader. Kroger's title for the person leading a remodel overnight. At Fred Meyer this role is the **Relay Manager**. Not part of your escalation path.

heading: Sequence (aisle sequence)
text: The order sets are laid out along an aisle. Your planogram sits in that order, which is why a set that appears to be in the wrong place is usually a sequence question, not a planogram error. The word is also used on remodels for the order resets and moves get completed.

heading: Set
text: A grouping of like items: pickles, peanut butter, laundry detergent. Also called a **commodity**.

heading: Set size (F / D / I)
text: The size field in a planogram code. **F** is feet, **D** is doors, **I** is inches. A frozen set reading D05 is five doors, not five feet. See Section 7.1.

heading: Shelf extender
text: A 7-inch metal extender used to sit a name-brand item next to Our Brand for comparison. Carries its own commodity code, 000.

heading: Shelf talker
text: A small sign calling out a sale, feature, or price.

heading: Shelf-lock
text: When a product can't go on or come off a shelf because the shelf above is in the way. Usually means a height is wrong.

heading: Shoe
text: The support the gondola is built on. Extends from the gondola along the floor and carries the base shelf.

heading: SKU
text: Stock Keeping Unit. The retailer's number for a specific product, size, and variety. One SKU can have more than one facing.

heading: Slides / glides
text: Plastic sleeves product sits inside to stay straight and organized. Used in specific dairy sets, canned cat food, and cake décor.

heading: Spans bays (⇔)
text: The symbol printed on a shelf strip when an item carries on into the next bay. It continues on the **same shelf number, at the same height** — the same horizontal row, so look sideways rather than up or down. The facing count on the strip is the **total across both bays**, not the part in front of you. See Section 7.7.

heading: SRP
text: **This means two different things, and context tells you which.**

heading: Store Intelligence
text: Formerly Rebotics. A verification tool that pairs AI with our planograms to confirm a set was completed correctly. It reads the section photos. Where photographing is part of your role, you submit in the app yourself and it tells you what needs addressing before you leave the aisle. See Section 9.5.

heading: Strip (shelf strip / shelf data strip)
text: The printed strip that slides into the data skin. Carries product placement, facing count, stack height, and POG data. In a DSL store it also carries the **tag size**, and it's what you scan to associate a tag.

heading: Sub-fixture
text: A fixture inside another fixture. It inherits the parent's number and takes a three- or four-digit code: 203 is the third sub-fixture on fixture 2. See Section 7.10.

heading: Surge
text: Extra reset work created by a new-item initiative. The reason a partial gets bigger than the notes suggested.

heading: SWAS
text: Store Within a Store. Enclosed areas in high-theft locations holding cosmetics, infant formula, laundry detergent, and similar.

heading: T-bracket
text: A style of outrigger used in OTC.

heading: Tag
text: The price label for one product, placed to the left of the product it belongs to. Technically a **UPL**. In a converted store the paper tag is replaced by a **DSL**; in a store that hasn't converted yet, the paper tag is still the tag. Check which kind of store you're in before you start.

heading: Tail
text: The merchandised portion of a manned checklane. Sized Medium, Large, or XL.

heading: Telxon
text: An old name for the store's handheld ordering and inventory unit, sometimes heard as *Telson*. The hardware line passed through Symbol and Motorola and ended up with **Zebra**, so the device in a store associate's hand today is a Zebra. If someone says Telxon, they mean the Zebra.

heading: Top stock
text: Overstock stored on the shelf above a set, and the name of that shelf. Maximum three high, above the matching set, labels forward, no heavy items.

heading: Travel strip
text: Slides into the slot behind the channel data strip. Unchanged by the DSL rollout — the slot is still there.

heading: U-boat
text: The green six-wheeled cart, narrow and U-shaped in profile, that Fred Meyer uses for vendor stock and backstock. Always walked, never ridden or coasted.

heading: UPC
text: Universal Product Code. The barcode. When the description and the UPC disagree, **scan the UPC** — descriptions are abbreviated and repeat across similar items.

heading: UPL
text: Unit Price Label. The technical name for a paper price tag — the label carrying the item price and the per-unit price. If you hear UPL on a call or in a report, it means the paper tag, not a DSL.

heading: Upper
text: Any shelf with prongs on the back that insert into the gondola. Different from a base shelf.

heading: Vendor
text: A company providing merchandise or service to a store. Includes us.

heading: Vestcom box
text: The weekly FedEx shipment holding planograms, strips, and tags.

heading: Wing display
text: A display flanking an endcap. The 3-tier basket hung on an endcap side is a wing.

heading: Zebra
text: The store's handheld scanner. Zebra Technologies absorbed the old **Telxon** and Symbol hardware lines, so anything anyone calls a Telxon or Telson is one of these. Used with the DSL app to associate and disassociate tags. It belongs to the store, not to us. **Leads: ask for it early AM, before the shift starts. No Zebra by mid-shift, escalate — don't wait it out.** I provide the login.
